utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Can we have the appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please, my name is Grant Niemann and I appear with my colleagues, Ms. McHenry, Mr. Dixon and Mr. Khan for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Appearances for the Defence, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I am Edina Residovic, Defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic. Defending Mr. Delalic with me is my colleague, Professor Eugene O'Sullivan from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I am Zeljko Olujic, Defence attorney from Croatia, appearing on behalf of Mr. Zdravko Mucic, alongside with Mr. Michael Greaves, attorney from the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I am Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo, appearing on behalf of Mr. Hazim Delic, alongside with Mr. Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I am John Ackerman, I appear here today on behalf of Mr. Esad Landzo, along with my co-counsel Cynthia McMurrey. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we have the witness? (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly remind the witness he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman, I think you can continue. DR JAMES GOW (continued)

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, your Honour. Well, Dr. Gow, good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As can be expected, still here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you have a good rest last night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, I slept rather a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you are ready for a long day of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As ready as one can ever be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let us go to where we left off last night, and we had talked about something you had written that appears on page 10 of your book "Triumph". Let me read it again. You are talking, of course, about the degree of detail that you have gone into in the book, and what you tell your readers is: "This degree of detail is necessary for an accurate interpretation rather than the more usual approach to analysis of the difficulties of the Yugoslav conflict, which relies less on analysis of particulars and more on opinion based on incomplete information and understanding." When we parted last night, you were ready to comment regarding that particular quote, so please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I was going to make three comments on it immediately. The first was that I would not take the implication of the final words of that quote as meaning that I understand that what I have done either to be perfect or absolutely complete and comprehensive; indeed anything anybody would ever do would always be lacking in some respect, I fear. The second is that it was addressed to a specific comment which had been made on drafts of the manuscript to the extent that it was very detailed and very long and, "one thing after a damned nother" by one of the reviewers, and I was putting this in as an explanation, saying that you had to have as much as this in in order to be able to get any kind of proper understanding. The third element was addressed to the fact that the vast majority, if not almost all the books that I had read, and articles and so forth, very often missed out crucial things, and one of the most crucial things absent, among others, mainly in terms of the dealings of international diplomacy, such as the fact that on 6th October 1991, the European Council of the European Union had decided that from then onwards they would be looking at the prospect of -- that they would eventually be dealing with the Yugoslav republics on an independent basis, or rather they would continue negotiations in the light of the right to independence, which is something that is generally not noted and recorded and therefore leads to misinterpretations regarding European Union actions in January and April 1992 and specifically also to the fact that many people, if not almost all, simply write things about events starting from certain points, taking no note, for example, of the declaration of Serbian autonomous regions, first in Croatia but particularly in Bosnia-Herzegovina in September 1991 and November 1991, all of which are crucial parts of understanding what actually happened. That is a comment I would make on the quote and why I put that part in the preface.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So it kind of had two meanings; number one you were in a way being critical of those who would arrive at conclusions about what occurred in the Yugoslav conflict based upon incomplete information and understanding and base their analysis on that and arrive at conclusions that may be faulty; and the second thing you were doing was trying to make it clear that you were attempting not to do that; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That in as far as the book was as long as it was and had as much detail, was that I was trying to make sure to include those things which were salient.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I take it that you are familiar with Lord Owen's book about his experiences about the Yugoslav situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you are asking me, I am, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That book, of course, was written more from a personal perspective, detailing his experiences in dealing with the international conference for the former Yugoslavia and the development of the Vance-Owen peace plan and things of that nature, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: One thing that we might be able to say about Lord Owen's book was that he sort of followed the same, maybe even more so, pattern that you were trying to follow in "Triumph", and that is being as certain as he could be about his facts; in fact accompanying that book was a CD that was published at the same time that contained a lot of the documents upon which he had relied for the things that he wrote in his book. You are familiar with that, are you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am familiar that he produced the CD ROM, I think a couple of times I have seen versions of it opened on people's computers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: One thing that kind of surprised me in looking through his book was that he relied upon and cited a number of other authors and commentators, like Misha Glenny, for instance, and so forth like that, and did not cite any of your work, which surprised me, because you had done such a large quantity of work at that point about Yugoslavia. Was there some problem between the two of you at that time or anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of any problem whatsoever. I talked extensively with his research assistant, Norbert Both, who later went on to co-operate with one of my colleagues, Junger Holnich, in writing what I would call the best book on Srebrenica, and also I talked intermittently with people working for Lord Owen's office, Jeremy Braid and David Ludlow, as well as other people in the Foreign Office. I do not see any problem with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We got very briefly into an issue yesterday that I want to explore just a tad more.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And also Graham Mesevi Whiting, his military advisor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: An issue I want to explore just a tad more, and we were talking about the difference between writing that might be done by an academic and that that might be done by a journalist. Do you remember us talking about that a little bit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: One of the things that you tend to find in academic writings that may or may not be present in journalistic writings is the extensive use of footnotes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is a difference, yes, most often.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: An academic, of course, wants to make it clear to the readership, which frequently is a bunch of other hypercritical academicians, that he has sources for the conclusions he is making and frequently the footnotes tell you what those sources are and where the information came from so that you can evaluate it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ideally that is the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So when an historian claims something to be a fact and footnotes it that is one thing, but then when an historian is basically giving an opinion, then it also is usually clear from the writing that that is what is happening, so an historian for instance might say that something seems to be so, saying that, "the best conclusion I can reach from the facts I have looked at is it seems to be that this is what is happening"; that might be a way to express an opinion as opposed to a fact, correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour, Dr. Gow said yesterday he was not an historian. He has been asked to express opinions on the writing and methodology of historians and having regard to his testimony on this matter I object.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me just ask him if that is his position. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I said yesterday, I am not trained as an historian. I deal with matters that derive from the past, I have some awareness of the discipline of history, but I think it would be most improper to speak, to make comments on history as a profession and a discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We can probably talk about academia then and separate it from an historian specifically, but before we do that, I then must ask you about something you have written in the introductory part of your book "Triumph", where you say this: "The second challenge I have tried to face is to provide on the basis of available documents, accounts and discussions a volume which will as far as possible stand the test of historians 30 or more years after the events combing the archives to discover what really happened. At a minimum, I hope the book may be a benchmark against which to test their findings. There will certainly be scope for improvement on the basis of new information which will inevitably emerge over the next 30 years." You are saying there, are you not, that you are writing a work of history that you hope will stand the test of future historians looking into this issue. Is that not what you are saying there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With respect, no, it is not. I think if you read it properly it will say that I am writing which I hope will stand the test of historians in 30 years time, meaning that when documents and documentation is available from archives that people will be able to go to that document as historians, in the way that historians would, and use the documentation and my hope, maybe it is a vain hope, but my hope in putting this together in the way that I have on the basis of the available documentation and of discussions, interviews et cetera, is that it will stand that test, but that is not to say that it is a work of history. It quite clearly does not say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So when you want it to stand the test of historians, you are not contending that your work is an historical work by any means, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not a work which I believe an historian trained in the discipline of history would regard as a historical text.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What is it you claim to be if you do not claim to be an historian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am an expert in war studies. It is an interdisciplinary blend of some elements of history, some elements of international relations, of politics, sociology. There is a complete composite blend of different things which gives you, in some ways maybe makes me a mongrel. If you asked me how I would usually describe myself, it is as somebody who does a lot of policy related academic work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Like a degree in international affairs generally involves training in history, economics, political science, maybe languages, things of that nature, so even though you are not following any of those particular disciplines, to an extent you become an historian, an economist and a political scientist all at the same time in many ways, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Or perhaps none of them, more pertinently, because you are something which is a blend of different parts of many of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Either way, you look at it, it can be one of those two possibilities, I guess. What has come out of the last few minutes of our discussion and especially that last quote we talked about from the introduction to your book, is that as we sit here today, and you are talking about standing the test of time, as we sit here today, there is a great deal of information about the conflict in Yugoslavia that simply is not yet available?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would suspect that there are things which will not be available until official government archives are opened in 30 or more years time. I take that as something which is normal, I take myself as being somebody who does their best to find out as much as what is available at the time. That is the kind of role somebody such as myself as an academic would play.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We have learned in your absence from this courtroom that there are Bosnian army archives that have not yet been compiled that are sitting in corps headquarters around Bosnia-Herzegovina that no one from an academic stand point has yet had a chance to peruse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That I am sure is the case and will be the case for those of many other armed forces, government departments in all countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It would be the case in Serbia, in Croatia, throughout the former Yugoslavia, there would be documents lying around that have not been made available to academicians at this stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not only to academicians but I suspect a lot of the time to some officials and politicians, government figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We know that even though World War II ended more than 50 years ago, things are still being discovered about World War II that tend to change our view of it almost on a yearly basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure that I would agree that things are coming out which significantly change our view, the general view, if that is what you are saying, but yes, there are always new things to be discovered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I did not use the word "significant", probably not significantly changed, but we are learning things we did not know before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are always small areas to be explored.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you are dealing with a situation in which you have "incomplete information and understanding", those are your words, there is always a danger that one could draw a faulty conclusion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is a danger that one might make some errors in terms of specific detail because there is a gap. It is possible in some cases that you might end up drawing the wrong conclusions from that. In this particular case, I would have to say that I am very confident about the conclusions that I draw, my general understanding, and that I would stand by it and as I put in the bit you quoted, I expect most of it to stand the test of time in 30 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I suspect you do. When you are writing an academic work, whether it is an article or a book or whatever, if you have reached some faulty conclusions, the most that may happen is that someone may point that out in a later work with additional facts that have come to their knowledge and although it might be a bit embarrassing, nothing terrible comes of it other than that you have arrived at a conclusion that turned out to be wrong. If we look through the body of historical work coming out of, say, for instance World War II, going back to the earlier volumes, you find conclusions in there that turned out, as a result of later knowledge, to have been faulty. That is a fair statement, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that case, you do, yes, which does not mean to say in other cases the same would apply.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It does not mean to say that, but it is not unlikely, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say it is less likely in something such as the Yugoslav war. In the Second World War, you are talking about circumstances which were shrouded in a good deal of necessary and general secrecy by all the governments involved. I think there has been far more openness of information in terms of the Yugoslav war, for example, than there was at that stage. I think it was generally the case in the modern world.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But with the Yugoslav case, there is serious question regarding the veracity and reliability of a number of the things that one can read about, the statements made by participants, the contentions made by participants, things of that nature. It is a bit difficult to sort out truth from fiction, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That may be the case if you do not have a sense of what is really involved and which things were going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When we move from journalistic writing and historical writing into a courtroom, which we are in now, where the result of a faulty conclusion can have a serious impact on the lives of a human being, we require a much more stringent standard of proof, and that is proof beyond a reasonable doubt, because when we get here, the cost of error is high, do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. Your Honour, Dr. Gow is not here to comment upon the functions of this Tribunal, and on issues such as proof beyond reasonable doubt. He has never purported to be in a position to comment on such matters, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually I know Mr. Ackerman is familiar that an expert comes to give opinions and does nothing more than that. The opinions which he gives are not necessarily binding.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I fully understand that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The question of proof does not belong to his own exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There is no question about that. What I am talking to him about is the factual basis of these opinions which is the important issue, not what the opinions are. Thank you. We had just very briefly talked about the difficulty of credibility and veracity of things that participants in this conflict might have to say about it. Are you familiar with the frustration expressed by Lord Owen in his book about that, where he says: "Never before in over 30 years of public life have I had to operate in such a climate of dishonour, propaganda and dissembling. Many of the people with whom I have had to deal in the former Yugoslavia were literally strangers to the truth." Do you remember reading that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sure that I read it. I also remember Lord Owen expressing that opinion on other occasions as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He talks with regard to that, does he not, about many of the people involved in the conflict in Yugoslavia having matured in their lives under Tito's communism, the communist system where truth was valued far less than it is in western democracies. Do you recall him making that point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you disagree with Lord Owen's frustration regarding the inability to figure out truth from fiction when talking to some of these participants?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure how I agree or disagree with his frustration. I recognise that he was frustrated in that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I suspect you must have experienced some similar frustration in trying to sort out whether some of the things people were saying about what happened really were true or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Have I experienced frustration is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: With regard to that, I suspect you have.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have had a degree of frustration. I think nothing to the extent of that which Lord Owen faced. Lord Owen was in a very different position, having to deal with people and to negotiate with them, which put him in a position where a lot of time, of necessity, they would not be telling him what he might otherwise know to be the truth. In my case, I will talk to some people and I suspect maybe some of the time you get a little bit more of an honest answer, because they are talking on a different basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Lord Owen was also a lot more deeply involved in trying to sort out what was going on and to draw some fairly far reaching conclusions upon which to base policy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that Lord Owen would desperately have loved to be in a position to do anything on which to base policy. I suspect one of his frustrations, apart from dealing with disingenuous actors from the Yugoslav territories, was also being able to get concerted support of the various governments in the international community supporting the international conference to form some kind of a policy or to support the actions of the international conference and of himself and first Cyrus Vance and then Stoltenberg as representatives of the international community. I think it is not on which to base policy, but rather try to do anything in the context of which coherent policy was not available.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Without naming them all, I think we can agree that virtually everyone who on a diplomatic international basis made efforts to solve the riddle of Yugoslavia wound up being met with frustration at almost every turn, up to and including Dayton and its subsequent time; still the frustration exists, does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Surely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I want to now talk to you for a while about the testimony that you gave on direct examination yesterday, and talk a little bit about some of the things you told us yesterday, okay? You talked about many of the conclusions that you reached in your testimony yesterday being based on documents that were provided to you by the Office of the Prosecutor, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is true that the Office of the Prosecutor made documents available to me and I looked at some of those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When were those documents provided to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At various stages since August 1994, since I began co-operating with the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Specifically yesterday you were talking in some detail about the events in Konjic and the Konjic area, and again with regard to that, you told us that you were relying on documents that had been provided to you by the Office of the Prosecutor, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure what you have in mind and therefore whether I made a direct connection between documents made available to me by the Office of the Prosecutor and whatever you have in mind, but it is true that in the beginning of evidence yesterday I did say, among other things, that I relied on documents made available to me by the Office of the Prosecutor and I can confirm that some of those documents related to the Konjic municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When were the documents specifically related to events in and around Konjic supplied to you by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have to check to confirm when that was, if I am allowed to ask anybody over there, I think it was probably about -- the first ones were probably around some time in September when the Office of the Prosecutor began to deal with me on this question and again in November, when I saw further documents when I came over initially expecting to give evidence at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were all these documents sent to you in London, or did you see them here in the Office of the Prosecutor? Where did you have a chance to peruse all these documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw the majority of them here in the Office of the Prosecutor, I was given some documents to take away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like at this point to request that the Office of the Prosecutor supply me with copies of any of those documents that might not previously have been supplied to the Defence, so that I might use them for purposes of cross-examination and impeachment. It may be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Which are the documents you have in mind? They may not know which you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The only way they would know is what I am asking for is the documents that they provided to Dr. Gow that were not provided to the Defence or not made exhibits in this trial. If there are any such documents, I would like to see them. There may not be. They may be all documents we already have or are exhibits in the case; only Mr. Niemann could know that. I cannot possibly know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are supplied with some of them?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The Prosecution has given us a number of documents since the beginning of the case, your Honour. I simply do not know whether I have been supplied with all the documents shared with Dr. Gow. If there are documents in the possession of the Prosecution that were shared with Dr. Gow on which he bases opinions and conclusions that he is giving to this Tribunal, then I think I should be entitled to see those documents so I can test --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are assuming that were some given to him which were not given to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have no idea, that is my inquiry whether there are or not. I would think Mr. Niemann could tell us rather quickly whether there are or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose you would not. The Prosecution would know whether they did not supply him with all the documents supplied to the experts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My understanding was that I was given things that had been put into evidence already which was why they were not introduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could I ask that the court enquire of Mr. Niemann about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, do you know whether any of the documents supplied to the expert were not given to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know of no documents which have not either been given to the Defence or tendered in the proceedings that have been shown to Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That is fine. I am satisfied with that, your Honour. You told us yesterday, and this is an answer you gave to a question from Mr. Niemann: "As I understand it, although Konjic was not a majority Serbian area, it was designated to become part of a Serbian territory on the basis of the number of representatives from the Serbian community in local political bodies. I am afraid I do not know what that figure is, but I also believe that the actual number does not make any difference, given that that was the basis on which they sought to act." I want to ask you from where you get this understanding.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I got that understanding from a document which I saw, which I understood to have been handed over or in evidence, but maybe this can be confirmed, indicating a number of areas which would be taken over, either on the basis of more than 50 per cent of the population in a municipality or on the basis of the number of representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you aware of the original source of that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The original source -- as I recall, it was a SDS document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. You told us that it was your understanding yesterday, and let me quote it so I can be totally fair to you: "It is my understanding that the SDS in Konjic provided, distributed around 400 weapons to Serbs in the area." Can you tell us where you got that information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Directly I got it from a secondary source, which is a book published in Spanish by a man whose name escaped me completely, the first name is Xavier, and I would not attempt off the top of my head to give you the title in Spanish. I think he quotes a source -- he quotes a source for a document presented perhaps in some other context here at the Tribunal or perhaps for the expert -- the commission of experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So it is just something floating around out there that made its way into a Spanish book that you have decided is authoritative?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I take it, I suppose rather than just giving evidence I should have checked exactly on the source and brought it with me, but I take it as being fairly authoritative and I have spoken to the author about the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay, "fairly authoritative". I want to write that down. Another answer you gave us yesterday was this: "I believe, judge, quite clearly" -- I have to go back a bit. You were talking about the decision that was taken by Jovic and Milosevic on 5th December 1991, okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was talking about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You were asked by Mr. Niemann: "In your opinion, what was their motivation for doing this?" "This" being the decision to basically split the JNA between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Serbia Montenegro. Your answer was this, and I again will do my best to quote it the way you gave it: "I believe, judge, quite clearly their motivation in doing this was to prepare for a situation in which the JNA units deployed in Bosnia-Herzegovina with a view to carrying out the project of annexing parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina for this new state project. After, any international recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina's independent international personality would be seen as a foreign occupying force and that therefore this decision was taken as a means of providing a way to camouflage the activity; that is to confuse the issue and to say, by formally dividing the JNA and by having primarily Bosnian Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that this was in fact no longer the same army, although it continued to have the same structure and to be left with all the capabilities of the JNA as they had been in Bosnia-Herzegovina before." On what do you base this opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I base this opinion on my general understanding of what has happened on the territories of the former Yugoslavia, and on the words in Jovic's diary which make it clear that they were foreseeing a situation in which the JNA, if it remained in Bosnia-Herzegovina without some step being taken, would be regarded as a foreign army on the territory of what would by then be a country with independent international personality and therefore they were taking steps to alter that situation. I think this is not an opinion which is solely my own, I think you will probably have noted in the course of your investigations into this situation that the United Nations Security Council also applied a sanctions regime against Serbia and Montenegro in May 1992 precisely because of the role that was being played by the Belgrade armed forces and others on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Before we finish here, we will talk at length about that. Right now, what I am interested in is whether in the diary of Jovic there clearly is not any language in there which sets out what the motivation of he and Milosevic was in terms of camouflaging, tricking, things of that nature. What it says is, "we are concerned about the international repercussions that would come from Serbian and Montenegrin forces being deployed in Bosnia-Herzegovina after recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina". That is what it says.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says that, and the fact that they are thinking about it and taking steps to avoid that, and the steps that they take in fact do not include the withdrawal of all the equipment of the JNA from Bosnia-Herzegovina, I think indicates that quite clearly their intention was to allow this project to be pursued but to attempt to disguise the project. I should point out by comparison that when the JNA was withdrawn from Slovenia and from non-occupied areas in Croatia and from Macedonia, as well as from the areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina not intended to be part of this state, all equipment was withdrawn. I think you can read from that a very significant difference in the situation which I, based on the fact that among other things the member governments of the Security Council judged was a situation in which this was what was being attempted. I have talked to many people who have been involved and I think most would agree that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You do know that there were, and we will go into this in more detail later, but you do know there were situations, do you not, where the Serb rebels in Bosnia-Herzegovina inhibited, prevented the withdrawal of weaponry from Bosnia-Herzegovina back to Serbia and Montenegro. You know that, do you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very little weaponry was withdrawn from Serbian areas in Bosnia-Herzegovina to Serbia and Montenegro. Most of it was left with units and most of that which was withdrawn was in the sphere of higher technology. They were only left with something like 40-odd aircraft, mainly aircraft were withdrawn. For the most part, the weaponry was left, in some cases there was misunderstanding and certainly some elements in the JNA at this stage were not, shall we say, in the loop on what was happening and I suspect, I am not certain, that General Kukanjac at the time of independence, commander of the Sarajevo military district, was possibly one of those, but I am not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I need to ask you the question again. You know that there were occasions, do you not, when the Serb rebels inhibited the removal of weaponry from Bosnia-Herzegovina by Serbian and Montenegrin forces; prevented in fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If it was not clear from what I just said, then it is the case that there were instances where -- relatively few, but instances where Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina tried to prevent not only the weaponry being removed but the JNA itself from going, as they understood things to be happening, which is not necessarily consistent with what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: With regard to the diary of Jovic, you told us yesterday that you had managed to get your hands on a copy of it, that it is kind of a rare document because it was withdrawn from circulation rather early. What I want to know is when you got your copy of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am afraid I can -- I do not recall any longer when I got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would it have been more than a year ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really do not recall. I could find ways of checking out and get back to you another time, but just now ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Please understand I am not seeking a precise date, I am seeking a time-frame.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand that as well and perfectly frankly, I do not really have a sense of the time-frame. It could have been a year ago, it could have been a little more, a little less, I really do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you think you had it in March 1997?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is possible, maybe probable that I had it in March 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you think you had it when you testified in the Tadic case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had seen it when I testified in the Tadic case. I did not at that stage have my own copy which I had consulted, but I had seen it and I was aware of the contents at that time. One of the reasons I introduced it now was because in retrospect, I judged it to have perhaps been a mistake to rely on the videotape evidence from, "The Death of Yugoslavia" interviews of Jovic saying the same thing rather than the diary entry, because the diary entry gives the specific date and we did not make it clear the point at which this decision was being taken, and the evidence behind the decision, when I was giving evidence in the Tadic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Those diary entries by Jovic were not something that came to your attention recently since your testimony in Tadic or since March 1997, but something you knew about prior to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was aware about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Other than the documents which you were shown by the Prosecution about issues dealing specifically with Konjic and that part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, what information is it that has come to your attention since March 1997 that you told us about here yesterday for the first time, the new material that you did not know anything about prior to March 1997 that has come to your attention since then. What was it that is new?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, but I am not clear -- if I said something was new yesterday, maybe you could give me the context for it. I am not aware of having said that and at the moment the question does not make particular sense to me. I am sure things are new to me since March 1997, but there are always new things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I am not aware either, and that is what I am trying to find out from you, if there is some document that has come to your attention, some breakthrough in knowledge, some new analysis you have done since March 1997 that changes your view since your testimony in Tadic or since March 1997. If there is, I would like to know what it is; if there is not, just tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Put in those terms, I am not quite sure that I understand -- in the back of my mind is why do you ask this, but as far as I am aware, there is no significant difference. I cannot say that no new information has come to light, but I have seen nothing which will change my broad understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, is it all relevant really?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, it is, your Honour. I am about to get there. Was there a time that you told someone from the Office of the Prosecutor that you had come upon some startling new information that changed your views about this situation that you wanted to come share with this court? Did you ever tell them that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall either telling anybody in the Office of the Prosecutor or indeed anybody else that, but -- I do not recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So I take it it would surprise you to some extent that the Office of the Prosecutor, in a motion filed with this court asking the court to grant your appearance here, suggested that there was new information that you would bring to this court that was not available in March 1997 and that that was a basis upon which they should grant your appearance here. That would surprise you, I take it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it would not surprise me. Can I ask, I am not clear; was March 1997 when I testified in the Tadic case? I do not recall when that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: March 1997 is when this case started.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. "New information" is perhaps -- I do not know, I cannot speak for the Office of the Prosecutor obviously, but I think it is important that there is the evidence that I have been presenting on both aspects to which I made reference, I think I am bringing evidence into this case which is not otherwise there, so I do not see why you would have a problem with the word "new" in that context.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You and I are interpreting "new" differently as we might interpret the title "Reader" differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I object to this line of questioning. Dr. Gow has not seen this motion and it is being put to him on the basis that he alerted us, or we alerted him, of new facts. In fact, the paragraph that I assume counsel is referring to is paragraph 2 on page 2, where it says: "Moreover, subsequent to the testimony of Dr. Calic, new facts and information on the internationality of the armed conflict in the former Yugoslavia and the protected status of the victims have come to the knowledge of the Prosecution." Your Honours, this is not a matter, if counsel requires clarification of the matter, it is not a matter which arises because of new facts that Dr. Gow can attest to. It goes to other issues in addition to the evidence of Dr. Calic, that was specifically intended to be additional to the evidence of Dr. Calic. I object, your Honours, to questions being put on the basis that somehow or other Dr. Gow solicited the process of giving evidence before the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: With all respect to Mr. Niemann, your Honours, the representation to your Honours was that you had to permit them to call Dr. Gow because he was bringing new facts that were not available at the time Dr. Calic testified regarding this issue of international armed conflict. Dr. Gow has now just told us that that is not true, there are no new facts of which he is aware that bear on that that he did not know about as early as March 1997. That is the whole purpose of the question and I do not need to pursue it further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Have you seen the testimony of Dr. Calic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did look at the testimony of Dr. Calic some time back in September when the Office of the Prosecutor contacted me about this matter. If I may, going back to the comment that was just made by the Defence counsel, say that I did not say that this was not true, I said that I was uncertain about it because I did not know -- I did not understand it was a reference to this motion, nor did I understand -- nor am I certain whether there is anything that is new to me in this or not. I just do not recall, so I think it would be unfair to say I said that it was true or not true. The word "true" is inappropriate, if I may say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If there were some startling new evidence that would change your view since your testimony in Tadic, you would certainly be able to tell us what it is as you sit there today, would you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you are saying "startling" new evidence then I do not believe there is any startling new evidence. I think I said, there may have been new evidence, but nothing which has changed my broad understanding, either since Tadic or since March 1997, but I am still not sure when, if anything new came into my understanding and any information either generally or in terms of what I have presented here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay, I think we are finished with that. Would you like to take the morning break, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I really do not see the need for all this argument, because there are differences between the Tadic case and the Celebici case. I think if he was giving evidence about similar incidents they will not pass us by, really, so I do not see any problem about whether anything happened in the Tadic case and something else is happening here. I really do not see the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My only concern, your Honour, was the representation made to your Honours by the Prosecution and the lack of new evidence that was represented to you to exist, that was the only thing I was concerned about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: New evidence to the Prosecution, not necessarily to him. To the Prosecution, not necessarily what he considers as new. It is the expert who is giving the evidence and he decides what he thinks is relevant and pertinent to what he is saying before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you are accepting it may have been new to Grant Niemann then I will accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes,.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: "Startling" is a strong word.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, it may have been too strong for the circumstances. Do you want to break now, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, we will take our break here and come back at 12.00. (11.30 am) (A short break) (12.00 pm) (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may continue, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, your Honour. Dr. Gow, in connection with the diaries of Mr. Jovic, you sort of mentioned in passing yesterday that the translation that the Office of the Prosecutor had given you was imprecise, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall if that is exactly what I said. What I said was that it was not a perfect translation, which I think anybody reading it would recognise, it was not a, shall we say, perfectly finished form of English. I do not think, as far as I recall, that there was anything imperfect about it in terms of conveying the meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That was what I wanted to ask you. Was it such that it would change the meaning of the language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not as far as I am able to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us yesterday the following, and the question dealt with the significance of the date 5th December 1991. You told us: "The significance is that on 5th December 1991, Milosevic and Jovic foresaw what the situation would be following recognition of the independent international personality of Bosnia-Herzegovina and therefore carried out a decision to enable the overall project to be continued, but in some way to attempt to be disguised." What I want to ask you about is that last phrase, "in some way to attempt to be disguised". Is there a documentary basis for your conclusion that there was an attempt to disguise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure about that. I am trying to recollect all the things that I have seen. I would say primarily that I draw the inference not from a document anyway, but from the facts of the situation, which saw the decision taken in conjunction with the JNA commander General Kadijevic, and I also made reference to the memoirs of General Kadijevic which are relevant in this matter for the intention for the plan, through two phases, to take territories in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina and also through the fact of the assistance, indeed instrumental use of -- sorry, the instrumental use of Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina by the Serbian security service and the continuing presence in effect of JNA units after the purported division of the JNA into two armed forces, and the continuing presence, even after that on occasions, maybe frequent occasions, of units from Serbia and Montenegro, so I draw the inference from the facts rather than specifically from a document. I do not recall if there is a documentary element in this or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You are certainly not aware of any documents that are authentic and clearly so in which either Mr. Milosevic or Mr. Jovic said, "what we were trying to do was disguise our intentions with what we were doing with the splitting of the JNA between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Serbia and Montenegro". That is not said specifically by either one of them in a document of any kind, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I recall correctly, in the Jovic interview for "The Death of Yugoslavia", my recollection is that he puts this something like in terms of sleight of hand, the way it is translated, which seems to indicate that there was an intention here to give an impression which was other than the substance of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We may have an opportunity to look at that as we go along here. You were asked the question yesterday by

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: "Was the role of Belgrade one of support or was it something else, or something more?" You gave the following answer: "It seems to me that Belgrade's role was to conceive of and to plan the execution of this project which would see these territories carved from Bosnia-Herzegovina to be attached to Serbia or Montenegro." This statement, "it seems to me" that you make in connection with that answer does not appear to be consistent with your rigorous academic discipline regarding conclusions drawn from facts. Is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not see in particular how it presents problems. I think, and again I say I think, I believe, it seems to me, what you are looking at is a case of looking at the evidence available and things known to me and having drawn an understanding here, asked as an expert to assist the Trial Chamber, I am giving an opinion about what seems to me, in my judgement, to have been the case. I do not think that causes any difficulties or raises any discrepancies between factual basis and the opinion which I offer based on the factual material, but maybe I misunderstand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I do not think you do. Let me ask you what specific document supports your "seeming" in this regard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which specific document supports my seeming in this regard?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You are saying it seems to you that the facts are such and such. What supports your seeming that the facts are such and such, as opposed to some other conclusion one might draw from it? Is there a document which directly supports that conclusion, or is it just the best you can do based upon what is available?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the sum of assessment of material available to me, either in documentary form or from events themselves as they took place, or from -- on the basis of discussions and interviews with people who have been involved along the way. I stand by that judgement entirely and I see no reason why I would want to change it, and going back to something you were saying earlier, I do believe, most confidently, that it will stand the test of time in 30 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Please understand I am not in anything that I am asking you today asking you to change your opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand that, I am just wanting to confirm the basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I am only trying to find out from you whether these are conclusions basically drawn out of a hat or if they are based on documentation that you could share with us, and that is all I am trying to do. I want to go now to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may add, some of the documentation has been shared, so therefore the documentation that has been shared, either in this case or in the evidence I gave in Tadic; it seems to me, this answers your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know of no documentation that you -- of course, it would be very difficult for you to know this, but you do not know of any specific documentation that might not have been shared or you might not have mentioned in your writings or something of that nature. It is your belief that I have everything that would be a basis for your opinions, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not say for sure that you have everything which is a basis for my opinions by any means, no, but I think you have things which show that there is basis for my opinions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just before you proceed further, I have here excerpts from the diary of Jovic. Does the expression "Sloba" refer to President Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You were asked yesterday by Mr. Niemann: "How would you characterise the relationship between the Bosnian Serbs and Belgrade?" Your answer was: "I think the Bosnian Serbs within the JNA and within certain political structures, and indeed associated with them who were loyal to this project, were effectively acting in the interests of Belgrade and pursuing a course by Belgrade, although in doing that, I think they may well have been undermining what would otherwise have been a genuine political question for Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but they were taking the role of acting for Belgrade against Bosnia-Herzegovina." I take it, boiling that all down, you are taking the position that the Bosnian Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina were acting for Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With the caveat that not all Bosnian Serbs were acting for Belgrade. In effect, those who were taking part in the Prosecution of this project were acting in the interests of Belgrade, and given the last comment -- the comment you included on the genuine political question, I do believe that there was a genuine political question for the Bosnian Serbs about their status within Bosnia-Herzegovina and the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but that question was completely pushed out of the way by the resort to violence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Referring only to those in that group that you just described, you would say then that they were acting in support of the concept of the establishment of a greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say they were acting in the concept of the establishment of a mini Yugoslavia, not as such a greater Serbia. I think if you look at the language used by General Kadijevic, it is clear that the concept was a new Yugoslavia, incorporating elements of the territory of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina for the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell me if there is a difference other than terminology between the Milosevic idea of a greater Serbia and what you just told us about Kadijevic's idea about grabbing a bunch of land from Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia and creating a Yugoslavia composed of Serbs? What is the difference there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure that it would be accurate to refer to Milosevic's idea of greater Serbia either. I would not want to get into unnecessary discussion about it, but I suspect also Milosevic would couch this in terms of a new Yugoslavia, a mini Yugoslavia, a lesser Yugoslavia, whatever qualification you put upon the term Yugoslavia, but one for the Serbs. I make the point as one of accuracy about their conception of what it was that they were doing. If you are asking me substantively, apart from the name, is there a big difference between a territory controlled by Belgrade for the Serbs called Yugoslavia or one called, as was proposed I think in January 1992, "Federation" or "Association", I forget, "of United Serbian Territories", the substantive situation remains the same, that there would be the territories involved and the population and they would be ruled by Belgrade. But the great Serbia is not what they would see it as being.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It is certainly not a concept, greater Serbia, that I just stood here and invented, is it? It has been talked about by academicians and politicians and Serbia over and over for years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Many people talk about great Serbia and the idea of great Serbia. My impression, without having done a detailed assessment of it, is that most of those who talk about great Serbia are not necessarily within Serbia or the Serbian communities themselves. It does not seem to me that it is a matter of great substance other than for the accuracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I do not think so either, when you understand that, no matter what you call it, the idea was to enlarge the area of Serbia Montenegro to include all the Serbs living in Yugoslavia, if possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you accept that the substance was to create a situation which would be the case, ruled from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This concept was not a concept that was limited to the minds of Jovic and Milosevic, but something that was a concept at large in Serbia at the time, and among Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was certainly an idea which probably could be said from the mid 19th century, but talked more pertinently from the mid 1980s, had been circulating in Yugoslavia and particularly among Serbs, the position of the Serbs in toto across the territories of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That would have included Serbs living in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Serbs living in Croatia, there was a great deal of support among some Serbs for that proposition, that there ought to be a homeland for Serbs, basically; a country that was composed of Serbs and pretty much Serbs alone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was certainly an issue in Croatia regarding the accurate designation of the Serbian community, when the new Croatian constitution was brought in in 1990, or rather the draft, which seemed to change the status of the Serbs from being a state-forming people, as they were to because of their position in Yugoslavia, to being something called a minority, another group, and that certainly caused popular feeling in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You do not want to back off of your proposition that there was a project to create a larger mini Yugoslavia composed primarily of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You stay with that proposition, and you understand, do you not, that that was not a concept limited to Kadijevic, Milosevic, Jovic, the powers that be in Belgrade, but one that has been adopted by Serbs throughout Yugoslavia, many of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a concept which had currency and, in some circles certainly, popularity in the conditions of the crisis and dissolution of the SFRY, that is the case. I think it has to be clear that Milosevic or Jovic or Kadijevic, or anybody else, would not have been able to pursue this kind of action without the material, the fuel to exploit. If you are asking me was there material for them to use in instrumentalising these communities, then I would say absolutely that is the case, in exactly the same way, maybe, that Hitler exploited Henlein and the Sudeten Germans, precisely the same situation where the population maybe had some questions of their own and issues to raise, but they were quite clearly used, in my distant expert judgement, by the Nazis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It does not mean then, does it, that because you are a Serb living in Bosnia-Herzegovina who ascribes to this philosophy and attempts to pursue that philosophy and make it a reality that you are necessarily tied to Belgrade in doing Belgrade's bidding? You are basically doing your own bidding at that point. You are part of a project that is universal among many Serb people, no matter where they are living?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a project, first which only makes sense if it comes with the agreement of Belgrade. It is one thing to be a Bosnian or a Croatian Serb and say, "we want this united territory of all the Serbs". That is not possible if Belgrade itself does not -- is not at a minimum open to the idea, or is in this case actually seeking to use the idea to exploit it, and as I was saying before, actually to move what might have been a genuine political question by fostering, by making the arrangements for the implementation of a project, military and political, which involved the use of force and I think the use of violence made it very difficult for that genuine political case to be heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It was certainly very clear during the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina to Radovan Karadzic, the SDS, the followers of Karadzic that in pursuing this philosophy, there was a sympathetic ear in Belgrade for that. That was clear, was it not? There was no question about how Belgrade felt about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was quite clear to them because elements of the JNA and the Serbian security service had been assisting them, indeed making the arrangements for them to carry out and implement this project, which goes back, as I may point out, when necessary the head of the Serbian security service could go and take control of any event regarding the Bosnian Serb leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us yesterday: "The Bosnian Serbs responded politically by formalising the Serbian republic in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was later renamed Republika Srpska in August 1992 -- sorry, in April 1992. They formally consolidated the Serbian republic in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which then later in August they renamed Republika Srpska, effectively declaring its association with Serbia and Montenegro, through the constitution which had been enacted in January 1992, and militarily, in co-operation with the JNA, they began the armed campaign to secure all major communications and access points into Bosnia-Herzegovina, so as to create a frame for military and political developments." Is that answer not to some extent inconsistent with what we were just talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not see the inconsistency.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If the Bosnian Serbs were simply the pawns and the puppets of the Belgrade machine, then would it not make sense that they would simply capture as much territory as possible, including as many Serbs as possible, and declare that they were part of the new Federal Republic of Yugoslavia? It seems to me that it is inconsistent with that idea that they would form their own separate republic in Bosnia-Herzegovina as if they somehow did not have ties with Belgrade, but had their own republic in mind separate from Belgrade. Is there not some inconsistency there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may help you, in Article 2 of the January 1992 constitution they specifically said that the Serbian republic in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that which was later renamed Republika Srpska, was a part of federal Yugoslavia they did this in the hope it would be possible to persuade Bosnia-Herzegovina to join with Serbia and Montenegro. When that did not happen, then in April the formalised -- the consolidation of the Republika Srpska -- if I may, I will use the term Republika Srpska, even though it was not called that in April -- the consolidation of Republika Srpska at that stage was to be a federal unit to be associated in this new Yugoslavia, so I do not see that there is an inconsistency at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There did come a time, did there not, when Karadzic and Milosevic found themselves at odds with each other and in disagreement, actually large disagreement between each other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a period in which Milosevic and Karadzic certainly appear to have been in disagreement, but I add the caveat that going back to one of the comments you made about Lord Owen, it is always very difficult to be sure with some of these people that which is genuine and that which is window dressing, but I do believe there was a genuine difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Karadzic, I do not know if you will agree with me or not, Karadzic kind of developed some messianic ideas and decided maybe rather than Milosevic being the leader of the Serbs, he should be the leader of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He may have done. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He certainly has acted many times as if he considered Republika Srpska totally separate from Belgrade and pursued totally different paths and aims, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there were differences between them, differences which can be explained broadly in terms of the requirements of Belgrade in the given international circumstances. I think, if I recall in Kadijevic's memoirs, he makes the comment, "realised as far as is possible in existing or contemporary circumstances", something to that effect. I have seen similar phrases I believe in biographies of General Mladic as well. It is the idea that there is a point, which, given current international realities, means this is the way it has to be. I suspect the differences between Belgrade and Karadzic and others in Pale was largely on the bases of Belgrade saying, "at this moment we cannot do this and say this".

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: For which you have no documentary support?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think if you were to go to reports of meetings, for example, in Pale in May 1993, you would see Milosevic reported as saying to the Pale, the assembly, that is, the assembly of the SDS, the Bosnian Serbs, "at this juncture, for the good of the whole Serbian people, it would be better not to continue to pursue this project. We have done all that we can up to this point, but now is a time to see the interest of the whole Serbian people, not just the Serbs in Bosnia". I think at that point, this is one of the points you can say there were differences between them. Milosevic was saying, "it is not in Serbia's interest for you to pursue this at this stage". The opinion from Pale was, "we are not happy with that".

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That was the time, was it not, when Milosevic was basically booed, rejected and run out of town, his ideas were specifically rejected by the folks in Pale?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure that "run out of town" would be an accurate description, but certainly the Pale assembly rejected this proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I do not think that necessarily means that Serbia withdrew all its involvement and quite clearly it did not, because it was still engaged in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yesterday you were asked this question: "Did the JNA operate in the municipality of Konjic, so far as you know from your readings? Answer: I believe the JNA did operate in Konjic municipality. It was there for only a relatively short period of the armed conflict, perhaps until May, some time in May 1992, although once specifically JNA units had been moved out of some of the areas in Konjic, I believe bombardments using JNA artillery continued." What readings are you referring to to arrive at that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Documents that I have seen in the Office of the Prosecutor, which documents I presume from everything that I understand are already in evidence, or have been offered to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you able to be any more specific about what those documents are and what they said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Documents include -- it is difficult to bring them to mind like this, but I think one document would be the interview I made reference to yesterday with Mr. Delalic in which he describes, as I recall -- I think it was this document and it was Mr. Delalic, but without checking I have to say I cannot be certain -- in which he describes first the taking of Celebici barracks and then later of Bradina, Ljuta as well, and describes this situation in which the JNA presence was removed from Konjic in this formal way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So that would be a situation where the authorities in Konjic were basically running the JNA out of the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I should also add that I believe it is the same interview, but it might be some other document, which points out that the JNA actually remained, or the JNA renamed -- remained and also was involved in continuing artillery action after this point. Ran the JNA out? I am not sure I would go with the exact phrasing, but it is certainly the case that Mr. Delalic and others seem to have been involved in activity which secured the removal of the JNA from Konjic municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Certainly by relying on that, you are taking the position that Mr. Delalic is an accurate and truthful reporter of the things that happened in the Konjic area during the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I made reference to Mr. Delalic's interview. As I say, I looked at many other things, I cannot recall all of them precisely in connection with this. There was nothing in this, however, which seemed to me to be either unreasonable or discrepant with any other information about that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I take it you have no documentation whatsoever or any information whatsoever to show that in early May 1992, the JNA, and I want to be specific and I am referring to the JNA, engaged in any combat operations in the Konjic municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My understanding is that the JNA units based in the Konjic municipality were not in a position to engage in armed hostilities because their barracks were encircled and under siege and had water, electricity supplies cut off to them. That is my understanding based on what I gained from the Delalic interview and other things that I have seen, and I base what I say on that, and I would stress that I make mention of the situation in Konjic only insofar as it fits into what I have seen is consistent with and fits into my broad understanding as an expert of the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I do not speak as an investigator on the question of events in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Niemann went into an area with you yesterday regarding a declaration by President Izetbegovic of a state of war on 22nd June 1992, in which it was claimed that Bosnia-Herzegovina was engaged in a state of war with a foreign power; do you remember that bit of testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You were asked: "What was the foreign power in which it was in a state of war with? Answer: The declaration of a state of war, I believe, regarded the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, so-called Serbia and Montenegro, as being the hostile power." You know, do you not, that throughout the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina the Bosnian government was making claims and taking actions in an attempt to induce the United States and/or NATO to enter the war in support of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you are asking me, was part of the Bosnian government's strategy to try and mobilise international support for its position then I think the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That is exactly what I was asking you. I thought I was clear, but apparently not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not the words you used, forgive me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Claims were made, were they not, that the Bosnian government had even shelled its own citizens in an attempt to attract international sympathy and support?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those claims were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you recall an incident on 8th September 1992 when it was alleged by, was it General Nambiar, is that his name, that Bosnian government forces attacked a humanitarian convoy in which two French soldiers were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall that report on that day, but incidents of that kind did occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In those cases, the Bosnian government, if what the reports suggest are true, the Bosnian government was blaming Serb forces, again in an effort to attract international sympathy and intention on their side of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not able to recall that specific incident, therefore I do not think it is appropriate to pass that kind of a judgement on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is it something I might perhaps be able to refresh your memory with, or is it something you have not ever known anything about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You may be able to refresh my memory about it. I do not say that I did not know about it, I just do not recall that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Lord Owen reports a letter from General Nambiar to President Izetbegovic on 9th September in which he said to Izetbegovic: "It is with a deep sense of outrage that I have to inform you that at approximately 19.30 hours on 8th September 1992 troops under your command attacked an unarmed UNPROFOR logistical convoy at the entrance to the airport. This unprovoked attack in broad daylight on an unmistakably UN humanitarian convoy caused the death of two French soldiers, injury to three more and the destruction or damage of four UN vehicles." Does that refresh your memory at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am quite happy to accept that that incident took place on 8th September.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Lord Owen indicates that: "The motivation for this action was that the Bosnian Muslims were trying to plant the responsibility for their actions on to the Bosnian Serbs, thereby portraying the Serbs as even worse than they were in the eyes of world opinion. This behaviour they supposedly could justify if it brought the Americans and NATO into the war on the Muslim side. It was the end justifying the means." Do you agree with that analysis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know on what document or other precise information Lord Owen bases that judgement, but I do not have a problem with the general sense that there were occasions on which the Bosnian government forces carried out actions, sometimes against UN, sometimes against objects on Bosnian government-controlled territory and the reasonable deduction would be that in doing this they were hoping to mobilise support, as I indicated earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This takes us back to those statements of Lord Owen's that we discussed earlier this morning, and that is the difficulty to figure out the difference between truth and fiction in what was going on and what people were saying in the Yugoslav crisis, does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It may do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Let me go to another matter that you discussed at some length yesterday, and that was this question that Mr. Niemann went into with you about what is a co-ordinator and what is the role of a co-ordinator; do you remember going into that?
