utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do. If I may, would you mind if I went back to your previous question, just to add something for clarification. You were saying that the difficulty in establishing truth and fiction, the particular incident you quote, it is hard for me from here, without looking into it, to say any further than yes, it is consistent with a pattern. I think more pertinently there was an incident in 1994 where British symboline radar with the UN force clearly identified Bosnian government forces firing in the manner you have been describing, so I think there are ways of establishing that these things did happen on occasions, so I do not think there is any problem with saying that, but it is easier to go with the clear instances where it could be established.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us go back to this co-ordinator business. You went into a fairly detailed explanation yesterday of what your understanding of what a co-ordinator was and what the duties of a co-ordinator would be, and specifically you spoke of John Hackett and his role as a co-ordinator in World War II. You remember talking about all that, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You opined, based upon your knowledge of the role of John Hackett in World War II, that that may help the court to understand the role of a co-ordinator.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I gave it as an example where I had knowledge of there being a co-ordinator used in military operations and the kind of activity that was performed. I think it gives a general indication of the kind of a role a co-ordinator might perform, but because it is not a normal term it has to be understood always in the specific context, but I think generic qualities can be shown through that role; the need for full knowledge and the need for a degree of authority, if you are going to be successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you actually believe that a group of Bosnians sat around in a building in Konjic and said, "let us create a co-ordinator like John Hackett was in World War II"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not believe that at all. I do not think I gave any indication that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I would guess that before yesterday, with the possible exception of you and Mr. Greaves, no one in this room had any idea what role was played by John Hackett in World War II as a co-ordinator; would you not guess that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you speaking about people within the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, people sitting in this room.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People sitting in the Trial Chamber, I would not want to presume, but I would not also presume they would know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It is a fairly obscure bit of information, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a piece of information which is more likely to come to somebody engaged in war studies than somebody sitting in a Trial Chamber or practising law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You do not have any reason to believe that a bunch of Bosnians sitting in Konjic would have known what John Hackett did, what his role was, what his duties were as a co-ordinator during World War II, would you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think as I already indicated, I do not think that they had any knowledge of it or were making reference to it, so I do not see that really is particularly relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It is particularly relevant, because you were suggesting to this court that the role played by Mr. Delalic as co-ordinator in Konjic probably had some relationship to what John Hackett was doing in World War II and that we could define his duties based on this obscure business of history that you dredged up here yesterday. Is that not what you were suggesting?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I object your Honour. That is a misconstruction of the evidence that was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it is not. I think that was exactly what was trying to be done yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness at no stage said that what happened with John Hackett was what Mr. Delalic said. The witness was merely giving an example to assist the court in an understanding of what the role was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I will accept that from Mr. Niemann, your Honour, and I will ask the witness this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I thought the witness himself explained. He was drawing an analogy between what John Hackett was and what the accused could have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I will ask this question about that: tell the Trial Chamber what it is about the actions of John Hackett as a co-ordinator in World War II that would in any way help them understand the actions of Zejnil Delalic in Konjic in 1992? How could that possibly help them if you agree that the Bosnians in Konjic and Delalic himself had no idea what Sir John Hackett was doing during World War II?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think there is any necessity of linking their having knowledge to the understanding of what the role of a co-ordinator might be and how it could be understood. I think as I made clear, and I think I made expressly clear because the bench while I was giving a general understanding of what the term might be by reference to Hackett, specifically said, "what about Konjic?", and therefore I proceeded to say that you have similar features in the situation. The lack of an appropriate regularised command structure, a number of what, I put it in quotation marks as "private armies", in the absence of the formalised command structure, units with different commanders acting to some extent independently, and the situation in which with that fluidity and degree of uncertainty, there was a role to be played by an individual with the appropriate qualities, the key ones being the ability to know everything, from each of the units what was going on, and the ability to have a degree of authority, therefore to be able to discuss with them, make arrangements with them, to be able to co-ordinate, defined by the same word, to be able to make arrangements for operations to be conducted or maybe in some cases not conducted where they would not be consistent with the actions or overall aims of others and to arrange for supplies and so forth. I thought I had made that fairly clear, but quite explicitly I was looking to similarities in the circumstances and under no circumstances was I saying that Zejnil Delalic, or indeed anybody else in Konjic, or probably anybody anywhere else in Bosnia-Herzegovina, or all the whole of the former Yugoslav territories, was saying, "Hey, what shall we do here, let us look at John Hackett. Hey, that is a good example, let us do it". It is something which is appropriate to the circumstances in which it emerges. I think that is what I was saying. I was not saying that there was an exact parallel either, I was saying the relevance which maybe would help to understand what the term "co-ordinator" might mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I take it that as you sit here today that you have no information, no knowledge, but what maybe the War Presidency said, "we need somebody to solve the problem of material and supplies between these various units operating in Konjic, could we get you, Zejnil, to do that?", and Zejnil said, "sure, I would be happy to do that. What should my title be?"; someone said, "how about co-ordinator?". It may not have gone any further than that, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First, I believe the indication he was already playing de facto some kind of role already. There was a document I saw of 2nd May giving him authorisation to travel and do other things, which I would note I think also said that where it was not paid for by others, at his own expense, which is one of the reasons I drew the conclusion yesterday that in performing this role, one of the qualities he had was personal wealth, and also probably the international travel facility, which enabled him to perform this kind of role. It seems to me that he was carrying out a role of co-ordination based on exactly the qualities I described which were relevant for John Hackett, which was then confirmed by the label "co-ordinator" on 18th May. To be clear, yet again, I am not saying either that it was derived from knowledge of Hackett and saying "let us do the same thing", or that it was formally understood in any way, but it was simply use of a label which was relevant to the role to be played which was a role which might otherwise have been within the command structures but those command structures were not available. It seems to me to be perfectly straightforward what I am trying to say, but if not I am glad to help you again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did the Prosecutor, in supplying you with information and documents in helping you to formulate your testimony before this Tribunal, share with you the full testimony of a couple of Bosnian generals who have testified here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you are making reference to the evidence by Divjak and Pasalic, then yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I wonder if you would not defer, since they are the experts regarding the Yugoslavian use of that term, to what they told us about their understanding of what a co-ordinator would have been; would you not do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am trying hard, I do not recall looking at it being struck by what they said in a way which would make me think, "aha, that is something other than what I understand". Perhaps if you would care to remind me of something, I might be able to assist you further.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you very much admitted to us yesterday and made it clear to the Trial Chamber yesterday that the term "co-ordinator" is really not a specifically defined, universally understood military term or position.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said, and I would not change my position, that it is not a normal term. I think I also said that I was not aware, and maybe I missed something in the testimony of Divjak or Pasalic of which you are going to remind me, but I was not aware of it having any previous use in the Yugoslav context.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, so the term "co-ordinator" in a military context really means nothing more than what those who create that position intend for it to mean, does it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think if you look to the record, I said yesterday it is a term which could be anything and nothing, but to be successful, whatever the specific duties and tasks involved, whatever role played, to make sense it would have to be based on -- it would only apply in unusual circumstances where there was not a regular and formal structure to call on, or where that was not appropriate and it would rely on the qualities of full knowledge and the degree of authority to be able to do something. It could be anything or nothing, but within that, to be successful, you have to have those qualities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you virtually conceded yesterday that in this particular situation it may very well have rested almost entirely on the fact that Mr. Delalic seemed to be able to have a trust and rapport among all the different groups that were operating in the Konjic area and perhaps it did not go beyond his ability just to communicate with all of those various groups matters that he thought should be of universal concern?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I think I lost track of some of what you were putting into what I presume is a question, but I would say --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you do not understand the question, maybe you would like me to repeat it. I do not want you to answer a question I did not ask you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you care to repeat it, I will try to keep hold of all of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It may very well be, as to some extent you indicated yesterday, that the position of co-ordinator was really based upon the unique ability of Zejnil Delalic to have the confidence of and to be able to communicate with the various armed groups that were operating in the Konjic area in terms of suggesting matters that should have been of universal concern to all of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think I would say that that was one of the qualities which was relevant, just as it was with John Hackett. A different person could not have done it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The other position that you discussed again at some length yesterday was a tactical group, and you told the Tribunal what your understanding of what a tactical group was and what its function was, and in doing that, you were relying on your general military knowledge of what a tactical group's function is in other armies that you have studied.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That, but also on references in the Vojna Enciklopedija of the old JNA, and the Vojni Leksikon, that is the old JNA which makes short entries for these things as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I take it again that you would not quarrel with Generals Divjak and Pasalic, who came here and told us what their understanding of what a Tactical Group was in the context of what was going on in the Konjic area in 1992, would you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of a way in which I would differ with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You would tend to defer to them on the basis of their understanding of what that term might have meant to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would defer to them if it was pointed out that their understanding was other than that expressed in the Vojna Enciklopedija or the Vojni Leksikon, which it would seem to me would be the understanding to be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So if this Tribunal is faced with trying to decide what a tactical group was in terms of what happened in Konjic in 1992, they would be better advised to look at the testimony of Generals Divjak and Pasalic, as opposed to what you told them yesterday; would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think it would be consistent with what I just said, and unless we went into other things between the two statements, I cannot say whether or not it would completely be fair. I would not presume to know more or be better informed than either Divjak or Pasalic, but as I said, I would want to know whether it was consistent with the use of those terms in Yugoslav military publications, quite significant well known Yugoslav military publications, and also the degree to which any of that has to be interpreted in the context of the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina at that time in 1992 when there was still, as I think I was making clear in evidence yesterday, an army which was not yet formed, was in the process of being put together, and given its structures and in which this particular measure of a temporary nature was used, as one of relevance. I think I also said in testimony yesterday, quite clearly, that the decision on 27th July to appoint Delalic not only commander of the tactical group but to say that that was all units on a particular geographical territory is not consistent either with Yugoslav or any other particular use of the term "tactical group" I am aware of. It is unusual for a tactical group to involve more than, say, five brigades. To put all units in a particular geographical area under control is taking it a step further, but I can see reasons why that might be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me see if I can find something we would agree on. Would you agree that on any view of what a tactical group is that its function and duties are limited to the functions and duties assigned by its creator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Wonderful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we can stop here and go for lunch and come back at 2.30. (1.00 pm) (Adjourned until 2.30 pm) 23 24 25 (2.30 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let us have the witness, please. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly remind the witness he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, your Honour. Good afternoon, Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us yesterday about another of your impressions, this one being from some documentation that you saw in the Office of the Prosecutor that there was a personal rivalry between Mr. Delalic and Captain Esad Ramic. What documents would that be that gave you that impression?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is difficult to say without having the documents to hand to refer to them, but among others, on the basis of having the impression that this was the case from an earlier stage, there are two documents dated August 24th and August 28th, the first of which says "I hold Esad Ramic responsible to me for this", and the second of which, three or four days later, is on the same matter but is directed to somebody else, I believe Mr. Mucic, bypassing that and includes the reference, as in so many other cases, "the order has not been implemented in the intention". I say this against the background of some other documentation or maybe from the interview that I saw earlier, but it seemed to fit into this pattern where I was suggesting that I suspect --- I can say no more than that, I have not looked into the Konjic situation so deeply or closely, but I just have this impression, coming as an expert and looking at the way in which events fit my broader understanding. I have the impression that that could have been the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. The best you can tell us is "impression that it could have been the case"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I made that clear yesterday. I have the impression from seeing things, I do not think I have seen anything from either -- anything which directly says there is a real problem here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You have raised again this issue, you have mentioned again these documents provided to you by the Prosecution. First of all, I suspect if you feel that in order to properly answer one of my questions you need to consult those documents again, that Mr. Niemann would be happy to supply them to you, and I think all you would have to do is ask, okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am happy to look at them whenever, if it is deemed suitable to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have no insistence on that regard, but if you feel you cannot adequately answer a question without doing it, then please feel free to request the document. I think you can do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, I think it would be a collection of documents that I would then have to see which ones I recognised. Again, I am quite happy to do that as and when it seems relevant. I think on the whole what I am saying is on the basis of assimilating all the various pieces of information available to me against the background of my general understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: One thing I would like to ask you about that process by which you viewed documents from the Office of the Prosecutor, did they supply you with basically all the exhibits in this case plus a number of additional documents from which you selected certain ones that you thought were relevant to your testimony, or did they simply supply you with a small number of documents that they felt might be relevant to your testimony. Which way did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure what the answer is regarding the first part of the question. I do not know if they showed me all documents put into evidence. They certainly showed me a lot of documents, or gave me the opportunity to look at a lot of documents. I have to say that there were very many of them and I did my best to skim through and try and identify things which looked as though they might be relevant as meeting points for my expertise. I would have to say that unfortunately, I do not have the time to have examined absolutely every document that was offered to me. I was given opportunity to look at a set of lever arch files like this or that, I cannot work it out, and I was given some indication as to some things which were in evidence which were found to be of relevance, but no more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Among those documents, do you recall that there were documents that were seized from an apartment in Vienna by the Vienna police that you looked at, documents that allegedly came from an apartment there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was shown some documents which I was told were Vienna documents, so I presume these would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So to some extent, some of the impressions and opinions that you have been giving us here today would be based on some of those "Vienna" documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is reasonable to say that I assimilated that information in shaping my views on this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you become aware in the study of documents supplied to you by the Office of the Prosecutor, or from other sources, that there were, and I am talking about the period of time starting in May 1992 through the end of that year, that there were several co-ordinators operating in the Konjic municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of there having been several co-ordinators operating in the Konjic municipality. No, I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You are not aware then that there was a co-ordinator for communications issues?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall being aware of that, but as I have stressed a number of times now, I do not regard myself as having investigated the Konjic situation, I regard myself as an expert who looks at the way in which elements come together in the -- with my broad understanding. If I were asked to begin work as an investigator, then I would look into all things of that nature. It seems to me that that is a separate question in trying to understand what a co-ordinator might be. The fact that there might be another co-ordinator in another sphere seems to me does not really make any difference to how you understand the role of co-ordinator.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I am really not trying to quarrel with you as what your role is as a witness here. I am trying to establish from some fairly simple things, and I am willing to let you take all the time you want to answer my questions, but I have no hidden agenda here with regard to these questions. My question is, do you know these things or do you not? If you do not know them, that is fine, you can tell me and I will understand there are reasons why you do not know those sorts of things, and that sort of thing. My next question is, did you know there was a co-ordinator for economics matters in the Konjic area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I can say and possibly pre-empt any other question of this kind, I was not aware of other co-ordinators. I think I already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Among the documents that were shown you by the Office of the Prosecutor, or that you had access to from some other source, did you learn about the existence of other tactical groups, Tactical Group 2 for instance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of the existence of other tactical groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were you aware that there was an "Operational Group Mt. Igman" that was in existence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am aware of the existence of the operational group.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Yesterday, not necessarily in response to a question, you went into some explanation about the situation in Nicaragua and the Contras and that whole issue there, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did, expressly not in relation to a question. It was something I was aware was an issue and it seemed to me relevant to say. I prefaced it, "if I may".

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I suspect you went into that because you are somewhat miffed over the Tadic Tribunal's decision and the fact it was based to some extent on what you view as a misinterpretation by that Tribunal of the decision in Nicaragua versus United States. Is that a fair characterisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is not a fair characterisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Have you read the decision of the ICJ in Nicaragua versus United States?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of the ICJ?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: In the Nicaragua case, ICJ, yes, you are correct. You are saying the right thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read that case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Have I read the judgement of the ICJ on the USA and Nicaragua case?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not believe that I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have any legal training?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no legal training, but I do not think I would deem to come before a Trial Chamber and try to express a legal opinion. I do not see the relevance of the question, if I may say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I stand at this stage because Dr. Gow expressly gave his views in relation to facts in connection with the Nicaragua conflict. The transcript clearly shows that. At no stage did he purport to give any view or opinion regarding the decision of the court, in fact that was never raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And because you do not know anything about the opinion of the court, I take it then you do not know that no part of that decision was based upon what the aims of the Contras were, and their activity in Nicaragua? I take it you do not know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I understand is not from reading that document. It does relate to at least reading in some degree the judgement on the Tadic case, and with no understanding as a non-lawyer for the legal implications, and understanding that my impression is perhaps not so much that it was anything to do with what I had in evidence but perhaps more to do with the construction and making of links and showing certain things were there, rather than that the evidence itself was there or not, leaving that aside, it does seem to me that to compare the two cases as a matter of substance, which I think is the point I was making yesterday or as a matter of fact is incorrect. What legal implications that might have I do not know and is not for me to say, but I do see that there are substantive differences between the two cases and I raise that, because it seems to me, somebody looking at it with a degree of expertise in international relations or matters relating to war, there is a clear difference in the two situations, both in terms of the nature of the activities on the territory of the country in question and in the nature of the activities of those outside the country who are deemed or are alleged to have been involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you have read the Tadic decision, you must know that the basis of that part of Nicaragua versus United States that we are talking about was not the nature of the conflict but whether or not the United States exerted sufficient command and control over the Contras to be considered a part of that conflict. That is what the issue in Nicaragua versus United States, as far as that part of it was concerned, boiled down to, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I understand that from seeing this, it strikes me that the factual material differs between the two cases, which is why I volunteered to make the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you again, the issue there was a command and control issue, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are still going back to the technical issues which perhaps is not your position to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the definite impression that I got yesterday from his testimony was he was trying to convince the court that US versus Nicaragua should not apply because it had different war aims than the Yugoslavia conflict. If he wants to sit here and give opinions that have legal significance, then I think I should be able to explore those opinions and it turns out, apparently, that his opinion is really not based upon any knowledge of United Nations v Nicaragua, or Nicaragua v United States. I will go on, I am through with that and I will start another subject.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may, what I said was based not on knowledge of the legal case United States versus Nicaragua but on some knowledge of the factual material involved in the case and that was what I was talking about. I hate to intervene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Those things might result in different legal consequences. This is what counsel is saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That I understand, but I also understand that to be a legal matter for your Honours or other people to decide who are expert in law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, we have taken fairly close to a full day to get this far, and I need you to know we have not got very far. I want to go into an area now that I am only interested in dealing with very broad generalities, I do not think any of the things I want to talk to you about right now are any kind of a challenge to you or your expertise or anything else. It is a small area of pretty much general knowledge that I need to put on the record of this case, and I really hope we do not have to get into long detailed explanations and long arguments about this little significant area that I want to go into. Let us see if we can do that. I am going to try to ask simple questions and I hope that you can either answer them yes or no and that we can get through some of this material rather rapidly, because we are going to get into some material that is going to be more difficult as we go down the road here. I want to talk just for a moment about the United Nations and the creation of the United Nations and see if we can agree on just a few things. The United Nations was basically born as a response to what had happened during World War II and the failure of the League of Nations preceding that, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It was specifically designed to try to succeed as an organisation of states where the League of Nations had failed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And an effort was made to try to repair some of the deficiencies that had existed in the League of Nations to make it an effective organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the goal always with the League of Nations and the United Nations was to create an organisation which could prevent the kind of things that had happened during World War I and World War II, to try to keep those wars from happening again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Broadly that was the primary purpose and one of the purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: A lot of the impetus for the creation of the United Nations was based upon the aggression that had been practised by the Third Reich, and the genocide that had been practised during that war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That clearly provided some of the impetus, but as you already said, also the failure of the League of Nations before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At the time, the people who were creating the United Nations were approaching it from a kind of hope in "never again" kind of philosophy, that somehow they could create an international organisation that could be effective in preventing things like the things that had happened during World War II?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the concept of collective security which underpins the United Nations was intended to try and deter the outbreak of wars.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you have anticipated my next question, the basic mechanism was that idea of collective security, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Based upon the proposition that if nations understood if they engaged in aggression or acts of genocide, things like that, the other nations of the world would be arrayed against them through the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: One thing that happened shortly after World War II, did it not, the United Nations with all of the work and effort that had gone on in creating it, was severely hampered by the existence of the Cold War and the veto powers of major players in that Cold War in the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is indeed the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When the Cold War however came to an end, the UN then, maybe for the first time since its creation, really had the opportunity to fulfil its birthright, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know about the "so to speak", but it certainly had the opportunity to begin to work more in the way that it had been intended at its conception.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Theoretically at least the idea of collective security could have some real meaning, finally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At least the idea of collective action to maintain international peace and security could; whether or not the actual concept of collective security itself, I think is a different question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: To some extent we saw how that could operate in connection with the Gulf War, did we not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But I think you would agree with me that the UN utterly failed in that mission with regard to what went on in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not agree that it utterly failed, I would agree that the mechanisms of the United Nations were more challenged than they had been in the case of Iraq and Kuwait. Many things took place which represented in fact if not the same kind of action as took place regarding Iraq, at least significant international engagement and involvement in an attempt to maintain international peace and security initiatives towards the maintenance of international peace and security which marks a significant breach with previous cases. For example, many people might point to the first world war, where incidents in Bosnia-Herzegovina provided the spark and a number of other powers came charging in using the pretext one way and another, so I think in that case, it would be fair to say that it was far from ideal, and in some senses you can describe it as failure, but to say it was an utter failure really would be to exaggerate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I guess you would probably agree that to some extent, the lack of a strong UN response to Yugoslavia was in some sense at least dependent upon a failure of will, to adopt some words of yours, on behalf of some of the member states of the United Nations, or a lack of will?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that is fair to say. The United Nations is an organisation, it has many elements, one of which is the Security Council. At the end of the day, the action taken is the measure of what the member states are prepared to do to address a particular situation, but the fact remains that they took in fact what I would regard and most people would regard as insufficient to the needs of the situation in an ideal sense, but certainly far more than I think anybody would have expected only a year before the dissolution of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, but even within the United Nations itself, there were the same kinds of setting aside any failures on behalf of member states, there were the same kinds of failures, and I speak most notably about the attitude of Boutros Boutros-Ghali who contended, as you know, that the UN had no business being involved there at all, that it was a rich man's war?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour, on the grounds of relevance. I do not see where this is leading us to. Whatever Boutros Boutros-Ghali said, or anybody else said in relation to it, I submit is not relevant to these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, sometimes the relevance may only become clear when one hears the final arguments at the end of the case and this is relevant to something I am trying to accomplish.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are actually making a statement which you expect him to agree with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That is the way cross-examination works, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Not all the time. So he need not agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That is absolutely certain. He need not, and I have no demand that he agree with me. I cannot. You know that that was a contention made by Boutros Boutros-Ghali, do you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am aware that Boutros Boutros-Ghali expressed a personal opinion that he had reservations about the United Nations as an organisation becoming involved in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I do not think that was the general assessment of those working in the UN organisation and clearly was not the general sense of the member states, the representatives of the member states making up the United Nations. Boutros Boutros-Ghali made a statement of that kind, but I do not think it can be taken as representative of the United Nations in any sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I would not suggest that. In fact the evidence is to the contrary, the Security Council did involve the United Nations in what was going on in Yugoslavia, at least to some degree, and in some extent to a fairly large degree, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Again I have another area that I want to go through rapidly and I want to go through it rapidly simply because to some extent it has already been dealt with by the testimony of Ms Calic, so I really think I can get through it quickly and we can get through it on a "yes, yes" kind of basis. I encourage you to try because we both want to get this over with.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Please understand I do not want to go into this in any depth, but I want to talk a little bit about Yugoslav history, because it is a basis of some questions I want to follow up with. I do not want to go into it in any depth at all. I am not going back further than December 1st 1918 when the kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes was created, you know that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was when it was proclaimed, not when it was created.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That is what developed out of the events that occurred during World War I.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the idea at that time was to combine the Southern Slav peoples into a single kingdom, partly to increase their political and economic stability and effectiveness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly the idea was to bring various south Slav peoples together in one country. Whether or not the motivation was for political or economic benefit is not really clearly to be said. I suspect one reason, if I may, one clear reason was more security benefit in some cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In that -- I will agree with that. In that Southern Slav community, there were three major groups at least, there were Serbs, who were primarily Southern Slavs, who became members of the eastern Orthodox faith through the Byzantine occupation, if you will, of Yugoslavia during a period of time; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, is that a fair statement that there were three main groups which were the Serbs who became --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That is one of the groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you are saying is that one of the groups, then yes, that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There was another group, the Croats, who were primarily adherents to Roman Catholicism?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That had a lot to do with the influence of the Austro-Hungarian empire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The lands inhabited by Croats were part of the Austro-Hungarian empire.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There were Muslims who became Muslims based upon the occupation of the Balkans by Turkey.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure what the phrase "based upon" means, but they certainly converted to Islam in the period of Ottoman occupation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That was what I was trying to say. Of course, there were a number of other groups, there were Germans and Jews and gypsies and Hungarians and Albanians and quite a number of different persons living in that broad area of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the case, if you are asking a question, also including Macedonians and Slovenes, important to the formation of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It became in 1929, it actually adopted the name of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Which I think literally means "united Slavs"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It means "south Slav land".

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: After 1929 when it became Yugoslavia, it was not necessarily a country that lived in agreement and peace and harmony throughout that period of time, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say it became the kingdom of Yugoslavia precisely because in the period before that, there had been significant political nationalist differences, including the assassination in Parliament of one of the Croatian political representatives and the declaration of a royal dictatorship and the proclamation of the kingdom of Yugoslavia was a response to that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Even after 1929, the Croatians in particular were not particularly happy with their lot within this Yugoslavia, were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The proclamation of a royal dictatorship did not take away the problems. You will probably know that King Alexander himself was assassinated in Marseilles in 1934 by a Macedonian terrorist acting on a joint operation between Macedonian and Croatian terrorist organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This 1929 version of Yugoslavia effectively ended when Germany and Italy invaded on 6th April 1941, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then after World War II, Yugoslavia was basically reconstituted by Tito as a communist state.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, as a communist federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And contained the six republics that we are all familiar with, Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Serbia, Montenegro and Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Each of these had a certain autonomy, constitutionally at least, and I want to emphasise that, and clearly defined borders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Each of them had formal sovereignty, although in the initial phases it was clearly understood that it was all a facade for single Communist Party rule. Over time that changed, and on the question of clearly defined borders -- clearly defined but not always precisely, because one of the things after the dissolution of Yugoslavia in some cases has been the question of delineating, particularly between Slovenia and Croatia exactly where the border fell. For Bosnia and Serbia, Bosnia and Croatia, for example, it was easy because the border was a river.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: From the time of Tito's creation of that federation, those borders have remained roughly the same up until today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those borders remained, as far as I am aware they remained the same from -- with the exception of the Slovene/Italian border, which was finalised in 1953, they remained the same, and from that point that also remained the same through to the end of the SFRY and beyond.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I told you I was not going to go back before 1918, but in fact just to -- it is kind of a throwaway here, Bosnia-Herzegovina, of course, had existed long before the formation of the kingdom of Croats, Slovenes and Serbs, whatever it was called, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina had been a principality within the Hapsburg empire and before that within the Ottoman empire, and before that there had been a medieval kingdom of Bosnia-Herzegovina with different territories. The territories of the present day Bosnia-Herzegovina were established maybe late 18th, early 19th century.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It has often been said, has it not, that Bosnia could be recognised as a place in which there was great harmony between the different groups.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That has been said, other people have also pointed out where it is a place where you could recognise periods of lots of trouble between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What I just said has been said by you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It has, I am sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The federal government under Tito was a constitutional government in the sense at least that it had a written constitution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And each of those republics that were part of the federation also had written constitutions of their own.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the federal constitution went through a number of changes over the years, did it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think it is the federal constitution went under a number of changes, but there were a number of federal constitutions, I think, what is it, four, 46, 53, 63 and 74.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The one that I am primarily interested in is the one of 1974, and the basic constitutional scheme of that constitution was recognition of the ethnic populations of Yugoslavia and a concept of proportional representation of each of those populations in the activities of the government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not clear to me what you mean by "populations" in this case, but I will answer the question in what I regard as the accurate way, which is that the federation was constructed upon the basis of the republics and of the two autonomous provinces which had been created within Serbia and which had also by the 1974 constitution been given a degree of autonomy; not equivalent with either the power and autonomy of the republics or indeed their formal sovereignty, and there was equal representation within federal bodies from the republics, so if by "populations" you mean from the republics, then the answer is yes. If you mean something else, then the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me see if I can be a little more specific. In the makeup, for instance, of the JNA, there was an effort in at least the officer corps of the JNA to accurately reflect the percentage of Serbs, Croats, Slovenes, Macedonians, Muslims that lived within Yugoslavia, so everybody would feel like they were proportionally represented in the organs of the state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was an effort to see that on the basis of ethnicity, which also sometimes was seen in terms of republican origin, that there was a proportionate representation within the officer corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that also was applied down through the various state industries that operated in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure that that is the case, because most of the industry, as I understand it, I am not an expert in industry, but, as I understand it, most of the industry was based in specific places, in particular republics, and was generally regarded as being the industry of that place, so you would have the Croatian electric and gas industry or something. I think there is a sense in which industries are seen as being from particular republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that this 1974 constitution was not a totally satisfactory framework to all the population of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be hard to disagree, because it seems, probably always was the case and certainly over time, some people came to regard it as being inadequate. In fact by the end of the SFRY, there was broadly dissensus about the continuation of that constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There was a feeling abroad in the land, for instance, that that constitution gave Belgrade and the federal government too big a role in the governing of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were two conflicting views, one which was that there was too much of Belgrade in the federation, particularly in the situation where Communist Party control had been devolved to the republics, so each republican communist party was now building its own fiefdom. There was equally the view held primarily in Belgrade, but also in Montenegro and by some other people, that there was not enough of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You have again anticipated my next question, and that was that there were those in Serbia who felt a sense of injury because of the construction of that constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were those who felt an injury because of the construction of that constitution I think primarily because of the creation of the autonomous regions, rather than because of the situation vis-à-vis the other republics, but the two things in many ways in the late 1980s became conflated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That became sort of clear publicly in 1986 with the memorandum of the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences, did it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again to be precise, I am not sure that it became clear, because the document itself was not put into the public domain at that stage, but it certainly became a prominent issue, the position of the Serbs in Yugoslavia, and particularly the constitutional status of Serbia vis-à-vis the autonomous provinces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It was certainly expressed in that memorandum.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the basic complaint of that memorandum was that the Serbs did not have their own country, that Serbia contained these two autonomous provinces and that this was unfair and that the Serbs needed to define their own national interests; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is an accurate statement which to some extent is fair, it might be a little more fair if you point out that it was written in the context of foreseeing the possible pressures for the dissolution of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The sense of the memorandum being that Serbia was not allowed by the constitution to have its own state, basically.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was the sense that Serbia was not allowed to have its own state, but I think that has to be understood specifically with reference to the existence of the autonomous provinces within Serbia which had a substantial degree of autonomy, at least by 1981. That situation remained formal in the case but de facto changed after 1981. Clearly that was a question for Serbia, how Serbia could be sovereign and yet the autonomous provinces, one could have representation on some federal bodies and two, could in many ways veto Serbian law-making capacities on their territory -- sorry, on the territory of Serbia as a whole. The idea is that law making in Serbia as a whole is infringed by the capacity of the Serbian authorities and Parliament to do this, it is infringed by the existence of substantial autonomy in the provinces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That was a contention in spite of the fact that there was a republic called Serbia which was inhabited significantly by Serbs, with the exception of the Albanians and some Muslims and so forth, but primarily it was a Serbian republic, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it had a population of something like 66 per cent Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The memorandum did not make the same kind of complaints with regard to the Muslims not having a state within Yugoslavia and how the constitution was unfair to Muslims for not having -- for there not being a Muslim state, did it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It did not, but I am not sure that I would expect a memorandum of the Serbian Academy to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Nor would I.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This memorandum played a role and maybe an important role in the rise of Slobodan Milosevic, did it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is often said to have played an important role in the rise of Slobodan Milosevic. It is certainly something which was contributing to the atmosphere prevalent at the time in which Slobodan Milosevic became first leader of the League of Communists of Serbia, subsequently he was to become President of Serbia. It certainly played a role -- it was an issue at the time he became leader, but particularly so was the question of Kosovo, so the two things went together.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you said with regard to the memorandum "this played an important role in the rise of Slobodan Milosevic as leader of Serbia", would you now disavow that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I would agree with that statement, but I would have it to be understood in the way I just put it. I make this distinction, because some people have put it almost as though the Serbian Academy document was produced and Slobodan Milosevic picked it up and made it a party platform. I do not think that is the case. I think it was an issue which created circumstances in which he became leader of the League of Communists of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You would not want people reading that statement in your book ""Triumph"" to interrupt it in the way you just suggested, but in the way you explained it, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I would ask you to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That was a terrible question. When I asked you if it played an important role, you had an explanation for that, yet in your book ""Triumph"", you wrote that sentence, that it played an important role in the rise of Slobodan Milosevic, without the explanation that we heard from you today and you would, of course, want people reading your book to understand that there is an explanation that goes beyond the mere words of that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would prefer that people did, but as the text you are referring to was writing about this in the context of setting up a broader set of questions and therefore was not going into it in detail, I think it is fair enough for them to read it however they want. If I were to write about that subject, I would take the care to explain in the way I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We are doing the same thing here today and that is to set up a broader set of questions, okay? In the late 1980s, Milosevic became the leader of the League of Communists of Serbia, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Prior to his ascendancy to that leadership, there had been some problems in Kosovo with the Albanians and claims of Serb minorities there, that they were being discriminated against and pushed out of jobs and things of that nature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Milosevic was sent there by the person who was at the time head of the League of Communists to see if he could deal with that situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It was during one of those visits that he made one of his speeches that has become somewhat famous and that was his contention to the Serbs assembled, where he said, "no one should be allowed to beat you".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was on his second visit within a period of five days, on the basis of having arranged for a stage-managed scenario in which this came to happen, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The effect was that he sort of stirred up that Serb minority in the Kosovo region at that time by those kinds of statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think as you already indicated, the Serbian community in Kosovo was already stirred up. Milosevic was exploiting that situation through the use of arranged situations set up by his people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But also he was making it clear to them that they could look to Belgrade for some support for their discontent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would think it was making it clear that they could look to him for support for their discontent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Once he took over as the leader of the League of Communists, one of the things that he set out to try to accomplish was to remove the autonomy of Kosovo and Vojvodina and to reintegrate them into Serbia, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And he succeeded in doing that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Although formally Kosovo and Vojvodina retain autonomous status, yes, in effect the powers which made them autonomous had been removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, and that really gave the reason that the autonomy remained in name only was because Milosevic realised that that would give him three votes on the presidency as opposed to one if he totally destroyed them. That was just a political move on his part, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This business of removing this autonomy from Kosovo and Vojvodina was not, although major war did not break out, it was done in the context of threats being made and it was a dangerous situation at the time it was going on, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a dangerous situation at the time what was going on?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That the autonomy was being removed from Kosovo and Vojvodina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It took place over a period of time, but when what I think was the final important vote, certainly it was one of the most important votes that was taken, it was in a situation of duress with military presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just to clarify exactly what it is I am talking about, you told the Tribunal in Tadic: "When the eventual vote on the removal of the autonomy or elements of the autonomy of Kosovo was taken, it was under a considerable degree of threat and elements of Serbian and federal Interior Ministry" -- I am going to start over: "When the eventual vote on the removal of the autonomy or elements of the autonomy of Kosovo was taken, it was under a considerable degree of threat, and elements of Serbian and federal Interior Ministry and I believe also Yugoslav People's Army armed forces were deployed in the area in and around the Parliament." Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You said it because it is true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said it because I understand that to be an accurate interpretation with the answer I just gave you before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: These developments that were going on in Serbia regarding the removal of autonomy from Kosovo and Vojvodina had a rather significant effect on the thinking of those in the other republics in Yugoslavia, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I judge that to be the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It created an apprehension that the leadership in Belgrade may attempt to expand its control beyond the borders of Serbia, then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It created the apprehension that the leadership in Belgrade was interested in strengthening the central elements of the federation, and thereby diminishing the powers held by the republics, and, as I indicated earlier, putting the Communist Party control at the republican level had created strong republican political structures and those involved I think, if nothing else, did not want to see that position changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it was at this point then that those in the other republics began seriously to discuss things like self-protection and perhaps even independence, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was certainly my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: One clear result of this concern, this apprehension was the formation of ethnic-based political parties in these other republics.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is true that ethnically defined parties emerged in other republics, as also they did in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, and then in 1990, of course, there were elections in various places and the Communist Party fared poorly, it was the ethnic parties that garnered the vast majority of the votes in those elections.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That really would depend on which of the Yugoslav states you were looking at. The revamped League of Communists in Slovenia in one sense did not do badly because the leader of the Communist Party at the time you are talking about was recently, the weekend before last, re-elected as President of Slovenia, so I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Kucan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Kucan. I think there is a varied picture to be painted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That was certainly the case in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the case in Bosnia-Herzegovina that the bulk of the seats were taken by ethnically characterised parties, although around 25 per cent of the vote went to non-ethnically defined parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There was also, was there not, during this period of change, a change in the law in Croatia which at least caused the Serbian population of Croatia to believe that their status had been changed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there were a number of changes in the laws in Croatia. I suspect you are making reference to the drafting of the new Croatian constitution in 1990, to which I made reference in evidence yesterday. If that is the case, then as I said in my evidence yesterday, that certainly was the case, there was a change in the constitution which appeared to -- maybe it was this morning, sorry, but anyway, earlier I said this, it changed the way in which -- the point at which the Serbian people in Croatia appeared in the constitution, which they took to be a diminution of status.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It was in response to that that the Serbian people in Croatia declared the two autonomous regions that you discussed with us yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not think it was in response to that decision, that decision was -- that constitutional change was a significant factor in creating the situation in which the Serbs in Croatia were unhappy. There were a number of other events, particularly in the summer of 1992, changes within Croatia, including a restructuring of the Interior Ministry, which was designed, on my understanding, to get rid of people who were communists and Serbs, the two went together. Were they changes to get rid of communists or Serbs? At the end of the day, the effect is the same, so these were also things which were creating apprehensions among the Serbian communities there, but the declaration of the Republika Srpska Krajina was not for a long time afterwards and the declaration of one of the two autonomous regions was again not for -- I do not remember the dates now, but it was many, many months afterwards, the declaration of the first was not long after this constitutional change. I think it would be unfair to give quite such a simplistic interpretation of it and say the autonomous regions were declared in response to constitutional change. Constitutional change was a factor in the political circumstances in which a Serbian autonomous region was proclaimed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you understand that I am not asking these questions in a vacuum? Let me share some of your own words with you, referring to that constitutional change: "It was certainly a move which made some of the Serbs in the Krajina area begin to feel a sense of threat and it was a situation in which, with backing from Belgrade and in some cases with the assistance of the Yugoslav People's Army, that local Serbs began to declare autonomous regions. In the course of 1990, they declared two autonomous regions, one of Krajina and the other of Eastern Slavonia, Western Srem and Baranja. In these two areas, they began to create, certainly in the area of the Krajina, a de facto no-go area for any Croatian authorities." That was what you told the Tribunal in Tadic and that is an accurate characterisation, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is an accurate characterisation. I would regard it as accurate. It seems to me perfectly consistent with what I said to you before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: These kinds of activities were the initial death throes, if you will, of Yugoslavia. It was at this point that Yugoslavia began to disintegrate and break up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that is a subject for an academic discourse on which point it finally began to break up, but clearly this was one of the events in the course of its dissolution, leading to its dissolution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We are not going to leave it there and you will have a full opportunity, because we are going to go into the break-up of Yugoslavia now, okay? I am sure you are going to get the opportunity to tell us what you want to tell us about that. If we look broadly at the dissolution of Yugoslavia, it basically came about to some extent because of the end of the Cold War, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Cold War was one of the factors which was relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, internally the glue that kind of helped hold it together had been a need for collective defence throughout all of Yugoslavia to repel supposed Soviet aggression.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Under Tito's rule, he was able to do things to keep a degree of order and in the years after his death, I think the prospect, possibility, however realistic, of a Soviet invasion in circumstances of internal division was taken to be a reason to find a way to go on with things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The additional factor was that throughout that Cold War period after, certainly after the break between Tito and Stalin, the west viewed Yugoslavia as strategically important with regard to the Cold War, in the Cold War context?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not of primary strategic importance to either the west or the Soviets, but it was of some strategic interest to both and its position during the Cold War was to some extent defined by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think I read somewhere that the west tended to view the territory of Yugoslavia as a route, maybe not a very likely route, but certainly a route through which the Soviet Union could invade Europe and there was therefore some interest in the west in maintaining a fairly strong Yugoslav army and a strong Yugoslav defence framework during the Cold War period. Did I read that wrong? Is that not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are a number of things in what you just said. Maybe I can help you. I believe that in the Cold War, the west saw three strategic questions regarding Yugoslavia, one of which was the Ljubljana gap, which I guess is what you were referring to, the idea that Soviet Warsaw Pact forces might come down from Hungary through Slovenia, through the Ljubljana gap and into Italy, so on the southern flank of NATO this would be a question. But the primary strategic question for NATO was always central front, central Europe forces in Germany. The second reason was as far as possible to deny the Soviets basing on the Adriatic coast of Yugoslav naval facilities and the third, as I understand it, was in the grand strategic realm of maintaining a communist regime in Yugoslavia, but a dissident communist regime which was not loyal to the Soviets, thereby serving to indicate that there could be more than one version of "communist" and facilitating the process of trying to undermine communist rule. I hope that it is of some assistance, for me to make this clear. That does not in all cases necessarily mean keeping a strong Yugoslav army; certainly around 1950 the United States and others gave some assistance to Yugoslavia to enable it to survive and not to come under Soviet control again. However, I would not be certain that by the 1980s, there was not a view and some reason to suppose that the Yugoslav army's links, whatever its links with the west and its position in between, its links with the Soviets were likely to be closer in the events of war than those with the west.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which is confirmed to some extent by the relationship between General Kadijevic and General Yazov in the Soviet Union in these very last days to which we are making reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to move forward in time. First we see the death of Tito and we see the end of the Cold War and we see the problems we have talked about developing in Yugoslavia and then we see the appearance of Slobodan Milosevic. Do you think there was a time when Slobodan Milosevic tended to see himself as a potential new Tito, a new Yugoslav strong man who could hold Yugoslavia together and maintain Yugoslavia much in the way that Tito had kept it together under the brotherhood and unity idea and that sort of thing? Do you think that he at one point thought that is what he would be able to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Be cautious in putting myself in his place and expressing what his thoughts and beliefs were. I am not sure whether or not he expressed something to this effect. I have a suspicion that he was interested in rising to the top and perhaps might have in some cases seen that, but it was certainly an impression that some outsiders, diplomatic representatives in Belgrade had in, say, around 1987/1988, where they saw him as the possibility of the new strong man, not necessarily a new Tito, but a new strong man who would be able to rise to the top and take control of the Yugoslav federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That was the thinking of the State Department of the United States during a two year period, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I object, your Honour, on the grounds of relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Initially being a fairly dedicated communist and adherent to this concept of brotherhood and unity, Milosevic was very opposed to the nationalist ideas that were emerging in Serbia, was he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, it is hard to know exactly what his position was. He was certainly adhering to established party principles until around about the time in 1987 where he went on these two visits to Kosovo and returned and thereafter seemed to adopt a new platform.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you aware of a --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may add, the real significance is in these two visits to Kosovo, because on the first of them he does spout the traditional Yugoslav communist kind of speech about it, and when he goes back, at the end of the week, it is a different perspective.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That speech in fact appears in the series of "Death of Yugoslavia", where he made that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe part of it does, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you aware of a quote that appeared in Vreme, where Milosevic said: "The appearance of the memorandum of the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences represents nothing else but the darkest nationalism. It means the liquidation of the current socialist system of our country; that is the disintegration after which there is no survival for any nation or nationality. Tito's policy of brotherhood and unity is the only basis on which Yugoslavia's survival can be secured." Are you familiar with that quote?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am familiar with that quote.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: As you said, it seemed that all of a sudden on his second visit to Kosovo, he had realised that the path to power was through nationalism rather than brotherhood and unity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That seems to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The backing that we just talked about that Milosevic had received from the United States obviously was something that gave him some courage to proceed with his efforts to amalgamate his power in Yugoslavia, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
