utterances.text: I am not sure I am able to comment on what backing he got from the United States and what he felt about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Again, let us remind you of something you have written. This would have been in, I think it is a journal called "Survival": "The US gave Milosevic its clear backing through the first two years of his rise to power in Serbia. This reflected the American hope that such a leader would be able to take charge of Yugoslav politics in the same way that Tito had. American backing for Milosevic undoubtedly reinforced the Serbian leader's aggressiveness vis-à-vis other elements in the federation." Do you subscribe to that statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour. Your Honours, I cannot see how the position of the United States vis-à-vis Slobodan Milosevic can be in any way relevant to these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose there are ways of getting round things. It might be a detour, perhaps he might land somewhere. I know it is fairly relevant, but I still have not seen where it is driving at. The cross-examiner might tell us where he is going.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: A number of these things will only become relevant, your Honour, when I make my final remarks to you at the close of the case, but I assure you I am not just trying to waste this court's time in dealing with matters I think have nothing to do with where we go in this case. I am trying to proceed as rapidly as I can through this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In September 1989, Slovenia amended its constitution, asserting republican sovereignty, did it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Once Slovenia took that step, whether you call it a fatal step or whatever you want to call it, once Slovenia took that step then all the other republics tended to follow suit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, generally each republic was trying to establish its position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At some point in that process, Serbia responded by proposing what really amounted to a new Yugoslav federation, wanting to continue a single Yugoslavia run from Belgrade, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. If I might just point back to the last question, when Slovenia took that step, it was also following the assertion of sovereignty in Serbia already, regarding Kosovo, as we had discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I am trying as much as I can, and I know I am failing, to build chronologically, and I keep jumping out of that chronology.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand it is very difficult. I do it a lot of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It is. Croatia and Slovenia during that period proposed, did they not, a Yugoslavia that would be more of a confederation, based to some extent on the European Community, a loose association of sovereign states?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whether or not it specifically could be said to be based on the European Community, although that is an allusion, an image which was raised at the time by some people, maybe as a matter of interpretation, but certainly they made a joint proposal for something called "the Confederation", which would be based on assuring the sovereignty of, call it political independence of the republics, as opposed to the Serbian idea, which would be a federation more of the old kind in which the powers of the republics would be concentrated in the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So what you quarrel with about my question was including -- modelled on the European Community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not quarrel with your question, I would just express caution about saying it was modelled on the European Community. The European Community was an image used sometimes to associate with it. I am sorry I said it, probably we should not be detained by this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You see, when I get an answer like that from you it just causes you to be here longer, because now I have to read you something you wrote in your book ""Triumph"", which is very recent: "Confederation was propounded by Slovenes and Croats who wished to reform Yugoslavia as a loose association of sovereign states" -- these are your words, Dr. Gow -- "modelled on the European Community."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those are my words and I make the distinction between my words and my interpretation. I was saying the image was used, and necessarily the intentions or the design and the precise modelling of those involved. I do not think it is a matter of great substance, I hope it is not, but if it is let those words be mine -- my interpretation rather than being attributed to other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I am just trying to point out that sometimes when you quarrel with the language of my questions you wind up quarrelling with your own words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not feel that I was quarrelling. Maybe at this point I am in danger of quarrelling, because I do not think I am quarrelling with my own words. It seems to me I am consistent with the words. When you put a question to me, I am trying to be accurate in answering the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You recall saying in answer to my question "I would not say it was modelled on the European Community". That is what you told me when I asked you the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would be interested to see the transcript. My recollection is that I would not say it was necessarily modelled on it in terms of those involved in projecting the idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This is beating a dead horse and I want to stop. During this time, western policy, to the extent that there was a western policy, it was primarily dedicated to the proposition of trying to preserve the Yugoslav federation, the state of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This position by the west had perhaps the unintended effect of supporting to some extent the aims of Milosevic and the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That seems to me to be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Because Milosevic and the Serbs basically saw the west as supporting their efforts to keep a Yugoslav federation, there was little incentive for Milosevic and the Serbs to be at all flexible about that proposition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That seems to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When Croatia announced and affirmed its own sovereignty in 1990, the ethnic Serbs then in Croatia began to react and we have already talked about how they effectively cut off part of Croatia and made it a no-go zone for Croatians and started creating these autonomous areas.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We have already talked about that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it was at this point that Milosevic began to understand that he was not going to succeed in becoming a new Yugoslav strong man and holding all of Yugoslavia together under his rule, and began then to talk about the sovereignty of the Serb nation, and announce that Serbs should all be united in one nation, and even though he could not have all of Yugoslavia, he was going to have as much of it as he could get as a Serb nation; is that a reasonably fair statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may, I find it difficult to deal with some of these questions because the way they are phrased seems to involve a little bit of a free-flowing, casual interpretation, the use of words which sometimes I might myself use as well in context, but it does strike me, and I really hate to say this because I do not want to get out of place, but in the context of a court and reference to something you said earlier, which I was not given an opportunity to address, it does seem to me that there is a burden in this context to take the language and the phrasing even more seriously than might be the case at other times and therefore to try to be precise in what is being said, and please forgive me all around, your Honours and everybody else, if I am out of place, but it does seem to me -- I have a difficulty with the questions sometimes because like this, the final phrases there --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, let me set your mind at ease. I forgive you, you are here as an expert, we are all interested in the precision. I am not an expert and I am not capable of the precision, so please any time I ask you a question that you need to lend precision to, please feel free to do so because what we want is as much understanding as we can have, not for you to buy into some imprecise question I might ask.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is fine. I raise this because this last question I could easily answer yes, but only on the basis that I would have reservations about the precise terminology.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you want to try to be more precise about the issue that I asked you about, or would you like me to perhaps read you something that you wrote in your book about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What you said in your book, and this really is the basis for that imprecise question: "Milosevic declared that the Serb nation was sovereign and that all Serbs therefore should live in one state, which meant that if there was not to be a Yugoslav federation, then attempts would be made to unite all Serbs. Neither Croatia nor Bosnia, where Serbs accounted for around 30 per cent of the inhabitants, could be independent without trouble. As violence gripped Croatia and Bosnia in May 1991, both Milosevic and opposition leaders made speeches containing the threat of war." So basically what I want to draw your attention to is the first part of that, the declaration of sovereignty of the Serb nation and that all Serbs should live in one state, and that sort of thing. That is where I get a question that is imprecise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you put it in those words, then I have no problem in saying yes. It was the terminology you used before struck me as being slightly different and looser than that, but I am happy to go with that and that quite clearly was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When I get in trouble with you is when I take what you say and put it in my own words and therefore in your view make it less precise than you intended it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hope you do not get into trouble with me, but one of the reasons we are maybe sometimes having longer exchanges than necessary is because I am trying to be precise than what has been said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I appreciate that very much. It became, after these kinds of announcements, and I am referring to the kinds of announcements about the Serbs all living in one nation by Milosevic, it became clear to the leaders in Croatia and Slovenia that any hope of working out some kind of an accommodation with Milosevic for any kind of a new Yugoslav federation probably did not exist.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that they drew that conclusion, they may have in some ways have drawn that conclusion before that time as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Certainly a very strong signal that there was to be no accommodation with Milosevic was the meeting of the Yugoslav presidency on May 15th -- was it March 15th 1991? I think it was, when Stipe Mesic was denied the presidency.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May 15th 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I am going to go back for just a moment to what we had discussed about the western policy, which basically wound up, intentionally or otherwise, supporting the aims of Milosevic and the Serbs, that is trying to keep the federation together. That in addition had the effect of, at least in Milosevic's mind or in the mind of Kadijevic or other Serbian leaders, that there was some legitimacy involved in using force in Slovenia and Croatia at the time that those two republics broke off from Yugoslavia and began to establish their own identity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not certain, if I take you correctly, that you can say that it was necessarily judged that there was legitimacy in using force to hold Yugoslavia together, but that there was support for holding Yugoslavia together and possibly an understanding that if force was used, there might be objections to it, but at the end of the day, it would not matter. I might add at this point, seeing as you seem to be relying fairly heavily in going through this sequence of events on the book, that since finishing that text, I have also become aware that although some of this is based on external appearances and the way some of the things seemed to be at the time, on looking at specifically a couple of other things, the memoirs of Warren Zimmermann, the US Ambassador to Belgrade at the time, and the Jovic diaries, to which we made reference earlier, it is clear that privately the United States was saying that, "we favour a single Yugoslavia, but we will never stand in the way of democracy". Maybe that was in the book, but clearly in the Jovic diaries, there are a number of cases where Zimmermann is delivering demarche to him about the possibility of using force, so maybe it is not quite as clear cut, on the basis of what I know now, as things that I said earlier, and particularly articles written in 1991 to which you made reference earlier, "Survival".

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you telling me this book "Triumph", which you hoped at the time of its writing to stand the test of historians 30 or more years after the event, is already starting to crumble?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely not, I do not think that this significantly changes that at all. I just say that, as I anticipated in writing that, new material would become available over time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. This would be a good time for a break, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I know we should rise now for 30 minutes for you to continue. We will rise for 30 minutes. (4.00 pm) (A short break) (4.30 pm) (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Dr. Gow, I am going to try again. What I am trying to accomplish at this stage is to move as rapidly as possible through some background historical material. I am not trying to be precise about it, because I think it is just background, and I do expect at some point to get into some matters which require a great deal of precision, and how long it takes us to move through this historical material really depends on you. I certainly would not want you to permit me to misstate something about the history, but perhaps we can move a little faster if you did not find it so necessary to quarrel with my use of language, as long as the general proposition is being stated rather accurately. I do not know if we can do that or not. I certainly want to try, and I will try and I will continue to try. The question I want to ask you now is this: it is correct, is it not, that in 1990 and 1991, western policy, wittingly or unwittingly, backed Serbia, reinforced its intransigence and contributed to the diplomatic impasse. Because the west wanted what Serbia wanted, Serbia and the federal army had little incentive to be flexible. Slovenia and Croatia decided that the only way to break the stalemate was unilateral action. Western policy effectively served to legitimise the use of force against first Slovenia and then Croatia after the two declared their independence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That sounds correct to me. I would also like to add something, just the thing you were talking about before the recess on this idea of threat or not threat and what I said about Zimmermann’s demarche. Also while there was concern about that at one stage, when Kadijevic went to Moscow in March he was assured by Yazov that their intelligence sources said that there would no such intervention, so from that point onwards, the situation I was describing originally was the case anyway. That is just a point of clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There were a number of statements coming out of the west and western governments that we are not going to commit any troops to Yugoslavia or anything like that. There really was, was there not, a climate of fear in Belgrade that there would be military intervention throughout most of the war right up through 1995; just as a general proposition that is the case, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there was often a concern, but a general proposition, I think there was the belief that would not happen as long as thresholds were not crossed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You talked a little bit earlier about Milan Kucan, the President of Slovenia. There came a point in time when Milosevic was prepared to make some kind of a deal in which he would agree to Slovenian independence in exchange for Slovenian agreement to change the SFRY constitution. It is clear from that that Milosevic was seeking to change the constitution to extend or change the interpretation of sovereignty to apply to the nations, the peoples, that is what he would regard as ethno-national groups, irrespective of their territorial boundaries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That broadly is the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What Mr. Kucan said about that meeting that he had with Milosevic was that: "It was obvious at that meeting that the Serbs would not insist on keeping Slovenia within Yugoslavia. We Slovenes said that we wanted the right to have our own state. Milosevic said the Serbs wanted recognition of this right for themselves too; that is all Serbs in Yugoslavia in one state. My reply, of course, was that the Serbs also had this right, but in the same way as the Slovenes, without hurting the rights of other nations. Milosevic replied, 'yes, of course, this is clear' and with that we flew home to Ljubljana." Do you recall that being a statement made by Milan Kucan representing his views of that meeting with Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to talk as briefly as I can about the efforts of the European Community to work out a solution to the crisis. There was an early plan, was there not, that came out of a conference that Lord Carrington chaired here in The Hague on 7th September 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The basic principles of that proposed agreement were that there would be no unilateral change of borders by force, that there would be protection of the rights of all in Yugoslavia, and there would be full respect for all legitimate interests and aspirations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That plan was, in many ways, similar to that that Slovenia and Croatia had proposed, a loose confederation based to some extent on the EC model.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I might interpret it that way. Others did interpret it that way. I think people in Belgrade did not, or rather they interpreted it in that way, yes. I will just say yes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Five of the six republican leaderships in Yugoslavia agreed, in principle at least, with this plan as suggested by Lord Carrington.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Five of the republics agreed to the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Milosevic opposed it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He opposed it, having previously agreed in principle to the terms for the agreement, which is why they had then put the plan forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He wound up opposing it because he said he did not want the Serbs to become national minorities in new republics within Yugoslavia, but wanted those minorities in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina to have their own separate sovereignty, those Serb minorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I recall, the Serbian delegation raised the question with the Carrington conference as to whether or not the Serbs in Croatia, one, could be regarded as sovereign and two, had the right to self-determination. I think that was specifically the question that was put to which the answers, as I recall, were they cannot be judged as being sovereign on the basis of a people, but that they may be entitled, in an undefined way, to some degree of self-determination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The Milosevic response to that plan and his objection to it was basically consistent with the deal he had tried earlier to work out with Kucan, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The attempt to make the deal with Kucan, which by the way Kucan did not actually make the changes to the constitution, was on the, say, basis of trying to ensure the whole of the Serbian people would be defined as sovereign rather than the political territorial elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The other thing he found offensive in the proposal was that he would not agree to restoration of autonomy for Kosovo and Vojvodina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have to go back and look at it to be sure. It is not my recollection directly that the restoration of autonomy for Vojvodina and Kosovo was part --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You said sovereign as a whole, without limitation of territory. Really I do not understand what that means, really.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I said, if I may, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I just want to understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The idea being put forward by Milosevic was that the Serbian people, Serbian nation, should be interpreted as being sovereign, that is across the territories of the republics of Yugoslavia, rather than the republics being the repository of sovereignty, so I think conventionally, the idea of, if I understand, the way I understand it is that sovereignty applies to territorial units rather than population groups and what Milosevic was proposing was that sovereignty should be applied not to Serbia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia, Slovenia, Macedonia, but to the Serbian people and that he would recognise the Slovenes as a population group in that sense, if Kucan agreed to make the changes so that the position of the Serbs across the territories would be recognised as one of sovereignty. I hope that explanation -- what he was proposing was to make the Serbian people across the territories be understood to be an embodiment of sovereignty, rather than the territorial unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually what is typically confusing is that irrespective of territorial boundaries of the different states --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You talk of sovereignty of a state, not of people. I was just wondering if I could understand what it implied. I have understood.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. If I may, in practice what he meant was infringing the sovereignty, changing the territorial position of other sovereign entities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let us do it this way again, Dr. Gow. I will quote: "With five out of six republican leaderships accepting the EC plan in principle, the only stumbling block was Milosevic, who rejected it, although this rejection was not completely out of hand. Serbia's chief objection was the proposed position of the Serb communities outside Serbia, having been classified as part of a nation in the old Yugoslavia, these would now become national minorities. Serbia's position was that these minorities should be sovereign. This corresponded with the proposal of the Serbs in Croatia. "A further major stumbling block was the quid pro quo for Serb political autonomy in Croatia, the restoration of autonomy for the Serbian provinces of Kosovo and Vojvodina, the removal of which had been Milosevic's central political platform, and the only real achievement since coming to power in 1986. Suggesting this, he said, constituted interference in Serbia's internal affairs."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is a perfectly fair representation. I might point out with reference to your question, which I was interrupted and did not get a chance to answer, there is a difference between something being included in the plan and the quid pro quo which was made clear, I think, to the Serbian camp, which was that if they were proposing some kind of status for Serbs in Croatia then this would raise the question, the quid pro quo, of the status of the province of Kosovo with its majority Albanian population. As I was saying, I would have to go back and check whether it was formally part of the plan. I do not believe there was specific reference to Kosovo, but that was understood, that the quid pro quo of looking at the question of autonomy for Serbs in Croatia was also linked to the same type of arrangement in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: To maybe clarify as much as possible these differences, the EC was basically operating out of fairly long established principles of international law arising out of an agreement at Helsinki and also exemplified by the history of the United Nations regarding the integrity of international borders. Milosevic, on the other hand, was trying to establish a sovereignty based on ethno-nationalism without regard to international borders, and that is where the conflict really was between he and the European Community and the international community, basically, at that point. Is that not fair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was a central element.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Could you just take a moment and tell us -- let me ask you something else. There was -- this philosophy we just described, that Milosevic was putting forward, was something that he was not necessarily consistent about, in the sense that he never expressed a willingness to apply that principle with regard to the Albanians in Kosovo, that they should have any kind of sovereignty. He seemed only willing to apply it to the Serbs throughout Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the case, if you wish I can explain why that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If it is important, you can do that, but it seems to me what is clear is that a principle that he was willing to apply for the benefit of Serbs he was not willing to apply to the detriment of Serbs and for the benefit of Albanians. That is basically what it boils down to, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it can be reduced to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Bearing in mind we are trying to move rather rapidly through material here, maybe we can be comfortable with that, okay? I do not know if the Tribunal fully understands who this fellow we have been talking about a lot, Kadijevic, was at this time, and what his role was. Could you just take a brief moment and explain who he was and what his role was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I did not explain during the course of evidence yesterday, forgive me, but I will be clear and expand. General Veko Kadijevic was the Federal Secretary for Defence in the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. He was the highest ranking man in the Yugoslav military, serving as a minister in the government, as a representative ex officio at the meetings of the State Council or Collective Presidency and as commander, subject to the supreme command of the Presidency, of the Yugoslav People's Army, of the armed forces of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Kadijevic was like Milosevic, very opposed to this idea floated by the European Community at that time, was he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Like Milosevic, he was opposed, though I am not sure that the opposition was based on precisely the same grounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He characterised the plan as, "Germany very openly attacking Yugoslavia for the third time this century", did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Of course, he also had a kind of personal concern, I suppose, in the sense that he understood that the adoption of such a plan would mean the end of the Yugoslav People's Army and then perhaps the end of his tenure as its head?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly the dissolution of Yugoslavia would mean that. Whether or not the plan necessarily meant it I am not sure, but he certainly understood that that was what the consequence would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I take it you would agree that with this statement, he also bewailed the reality that the plan would mean the end of the federal army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you have expressed your conclusion about this next issue with such frequency that we can deal with it rather rapidly. You have taken the position on numerous occasions that Yugoslavia ceased to exist on 15th May 1991 when Stipe Mesic was not permitted to take his seat as President of the Presidency of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I may have expressed that judgement. As I recall, there was a question about this in the Tadic case, and I think what I said there was that I think from that point onwards, the SFRY ceased to function, but that the SFRY ultimately can formally be said to have ceased to exist on 27th April 1992. I am saying this in line with the opinions of the Badinter Advisory Commission to the European Community conference, you made reference before, here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Who was Mesic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stipe Mesic was the designated Croatian representative to the State Council, otherwise known as the Collective Presidency. This was a point at which representatives from each of the six republics, plus a representative from each of the two autonomous provinces within Serbia, came together. The Defence Secretary Kadijevic would also attend the meetings. Mesic was due on 15th May 1991 to rotate to being President of this Council in what had otherwise always been a formality, but on this occasion, the vote to confirm this was blocked. The reason why I take 15th May as being the date on which the SFRY effectively ceased to function is precisely because of this blockage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Ceasing to function in many ways is synonymous with ceasing to exist. It could not function as a federation any longer, so therefore really it did not have any effective existence from that point forward, did it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be my judgement, but the issue is not straightforward, as I think I just made clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That has been your judgement on a number of occasions. You have I think been careful on each occasion to use the words "ceased to function" as opposed to ceased to exist, but certainly you would not quarrel with the proposition that by April 1992 that it ceased to exist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Certainly by May 1st 1992, there was no SFRY.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. By May 1st 1992, the federal authorities in Belgrade only had control at that point legally over matters within Serbia and Montenegro. That is the only place they could exercise control as a government.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbia and Montenegro were the republics which were said to form the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The sovereignty of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia did not extend beyond the borders of Serbia and Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This was by this time recognised as a fact at least, and I am not suggesting diplomatic recognition of FRY, I am just recognising de facto that Serbia and Montenegro was now its own separate little fiefdom, that its sovereignty was confined to those two countries.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There had been, had there not, significantly prior to this agreement by Milosevic, even though he took different positions now and then, in October 1991 he agreed that the borders of the republics were to be respected, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on 4th October 1991 he agreed in principle to the idea of territorial integrity for the republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When it became clear to the European Community that Yugoslavia was dissolving and that there were yearnings for independence on the part of Slovenia, Croatia and perhaps other republics, a response that the EC fashioned to that was to create a commission to study that called, and I cannot pronounce this man's name, I think it is Badinter, or something like that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The EC organised the conference in The Hague and the advisory commission, under French jurist Robert Badinter was assigned to advise on legal matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That commission was basically tasked to advise the EC on what the conditions should be under which recognition would be extended to these proposed republics, proposed independent states.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The commission was established to give opinions to the conference, in particular to the conference chair Lord Carrington on questions that he raised. For example, when the Serbian delegation raised the question we discussed earlier on, sovereignty of Serbs or the right to self-determination, that was then a question which Carrington put to the commission to get an advisory opinion upon and that was the basis for it. At a later stage, if I think -- maybe now I am just realising what you are talking about, as part of this process, when the EC in December 1991 decided to invite those Yugoslav republics seeking recognition as having independent international personality to do so, then also the EC Council in this case through the conference asked Badinter Advisory Commission to assess the applications vis-à-vis a number of possible guidelines for whether or not it would be appropriate to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Is it the same commission which Dr. Calic described as "arbitration commission"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She might well. I would have to check the transcript as to what Dr. Calic called it. But it was the advisory commission to the European Conference on Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This commission, this Badinter Commission in fact proposed to the Council guidelines that the Council should apply in determining whether or not to extend recognition to these fledgling states.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were guidelines and the advisory commission gave opinions on the applications.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There came a point, did there not, where the EC Council met and agreed to follow the vision of the commission regarding these guidelines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure what you have in mind. I will say anyway, the European Council met on 16th going through into the night of 17th December 1991, at which it was agreed to draw up these guidelines and to suggest the invitation or possibility of having recognition of independent international personality. Then on 15th January 1992, the European Council met to discuss the opinions offered by the advisory commission and then proceeded to make political decisions on the basis of those opinions, but not entirely on the basis of those opinions, given that one of the opinions was that Macedonia should be recognised, but for political reasons that did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I seem to always be able to be more precise when I read your words to you, so I will do that: "Only one week after establishing a common EC policy, including the process of taking advice from the Badinter Commission and the priority of acting jointly, Bonn", that would be the German government, "announced on 23rd December 1991 that it would recognise Slovenia and Croatia and establish diplomatic links on 15th January."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In effect what happened there was the German government, having agreed that they would go through this Badinter process, then, for whatever reason, and there are reasons we could discuss and I do not think we need to, but for whatever reason, basically the German government said, "we are going to go ahead and recognise as of January 15th". That is what happened, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What was going on at that point with the EC was a very deliberate and careful effort to try to methodically go through this process in a way to try to avoid the breaking out of armed hostilities, when the recognitions finally came about, to try to establish a framework, an understanding, a way to do this, to minimise as much as possible the possibility of war breaking out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the EC, as was the case with all other international actors, wanted to limit any possibilities of armed hostilities, or the scope of armed hostilities. Again, forgive me for doing what you say is quarrelling, but I do not believe I am quarrelling with you, I am just seeking to be clear, armed hostilities had been taking place in Croatia, which is one of the countries in question, for some six months by this stage, so I do not think it was any question of the EC in doing this attempting to prevent the possibilities of armed hostilities. They were actually taking place, so whilst there was a general desire always to prevent armed hostilities, that would have been filtered into this process. If I understood you correctly, or heard you correctly, I do not think you could say that this was the motivation in carrying out the work of this meeting of the European Council. I think what it was was a way of managing the process of dissolution of the SFRY, primarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There was certainly a sense, was there not, that -- and we are talking about some fairly sensitive diplomatic work that was going on here during this time, there was a sense, was there not, in the EC that by going about this through the use of the Badinter Commission and being careful and deliberate about it, that not only might the process end, the hostilities that were going on in Croatia, but also prevent the outbreak of a wider Yugoslavian war. Was that not on the minds of the people that were trying to work through this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think they certainly hoped that whatever they did would be able to prevent that, but it was a significant issue of dispute, even at the European Council meeting in December, to which I made reference, between those who felt that the way to do this would be to move sooner rather than later towards recognition of independent international personality and those who thought it might be better to delay the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you will agree at least that several commentators have seen the rather precipitous action of the German government as perhaps contributing to the breakout of a wider war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would agree that a number of commentators have made that observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I am going to fast forward a bit now, and I want to concentrate a little bit on events that were occurring in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is not necessarily forward in time, but forward in subject matter. I want to direct your attention to October 1991, and activities that were going on in the Bosnian Parliament at that time. At that stage, the Parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina affirmed the sovereign state quality of Bosnia-Herzegovina, indicating them to be a state of equal citizens and peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina; that is the Muslims, the Slav Muslims, the Serbs and the Croats, as well as any other population groups living on the territories. That happened in October 1991, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At that time, in that Parliament, representing the SDS was a fellow by the name of Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time Karadzic was leader of the SDS in the Bosnian Parliament, although at the precise time of the adoption of the platform on sovereignty, it is my recollection that Karadzic had led the SDS delegates out of the chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On October 14th 1991, expressing his opposition to this idea of sovereignty for Bosnia-Herzegovina, he actually took the podium and made a speech, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to quote his words, tell me if you believe I am quoting him accurately: "You want to take Bosnia and Herzegovina down the same highway of hell and suffering that Slovenia and Croatia are travelling. Do not think that you will not lead Bosnia and Herzegovina into hell and do not think that you will perhaps make the Muslim people disappear, because the Muslims cannot defend themselves if there is war. How will you prevent everyone from being killed in Bosnia and Herzegovina?" Right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Fairly provocative words, are they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They appear to be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: President Izetbegovic felt it necessary to reply to that outburst by saying: "As President of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I am sorry that in this situation I must talk for the Muslim people. I solemnly state that the Muslims will not attack anyone. However, just as solemnly, I state that the Muslims will defend themselves with great determination and survive. They will not disappear as Karadzic said, they cannot disappear." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It might be helpful to their Honours if I also add that this discussion on the platform on sovereignty was taking place against the background of the declaration of the Serbian autonomous regions to which I made reference earlier in testimony, which took place in September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And the vision that was in the mind of Karadzic at that point, some of which had already been carried into effect by declaration, was for a large piece of Bosnia-Herzegovina to become purely Serb and perhaps link up with FRY and become part of FRY.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be my judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There were, however, large numbers of Serbs living in Bosnia-Herzegovina that rejected this vision of Karadzic, did they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were certainly good numbers of Serbs who did not necessarily support this Karadzic vision, even some members of the SDS, for example, at later stages when they began to see exactly what was happening, left the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You have written in your book, and I think there may very well be a proof reading problem with this sentence, which you recognise as a problem many places in "Triumph", do you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I fear I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I do not want to embarrass you about that and I am not trying to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not going into it, but I think it is not necessarily a question of proof reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I do not want to go into it either, but perhaps you can clarify this sentence, because it is not clear the way it is written in your book: "It should not be assumed, however, that all the Serbs held to the Karadzic line; clearly tens, if not hundreds, of thousands of them rejected his vision." I do not understand that, whether it is saying ten Serbs or hundred Serbs or 100,000 Serbs. What was the number you were trying to state there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Forgive me if I was not clear, but I was indicating that maybe it would be better expressed as tens of thousands of Serbs, possibly hundreds of thousands of them, did not opt for the Karadzic vision, although I do not think there is a way to be precise about the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That is the way I read it, but I was not certain. There were even Serbs serving in the Parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina who supported the Izetbegovic position and favoured the holding of the referendum that had been recommended by the Badinter Commission, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Karadzic, of course, opposed the holding of that referendum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The referendum in fact took place on February 29th and 1st March 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 64.4 per cent of the Bosnian population voted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is probably the figure. As I do not have it to hand and I have not rehearsed I cannot be sure, something of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you understand that I am trying to be accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do understand, which is why I am careful, because I do not have a figure in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Of that number, 99.7 per cent voted in favour of independence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That seems to me to be right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There has been subsequent claim by Serbs that the referendum was not valid because they had boycotted that referendum.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In fact the SDS announced a boycott of the referendum.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: More than announcing and encouraging Serbs to boycott it, they took active steps to prevent Serbs from voting in that referendum, did they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They erected barriers so that ballot boxes could not get to polling places where Serbs were likely to vote.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was reported to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you would agree with me that under ordinary democratic principles, this referendum was in fact binding on the entire population of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think you said "ordinary democratic principles", but I am not quite sure what ordinary democratic principles are. Referendums are held on a number of different bases, requiring different types of majority. It is my judgement, derived from the opinion of the advisory commission we discussed, that this was appropriate and binding in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Ordinary democratic principles going all the way back to ancient Greece tend to be based on the proposition of majority rule; that is a fair statement, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is one of the elements of democracy. Also if you are talking about referendums, sometimes particular benchmarks are set.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In this case, there were none.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The Serb position that because a minority refused to vote, would be absurd, could defeat a referendum because a minority refused to vote would be absurd, because what you are then looking at is rule by minority rather than majority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be the case in what you might describe as an ordinary situation. In the context of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Serbs also made this claim on the basis of a constitutional amendment in 1990, equating all the constituent peoples and therefore argued that because a number of the Serbs had not participated in the referendum then it should be regarded as being invalid, but that is not the opinion that was taken by the advisory commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It is real interesting to bar people from voting and then claim because they did not vote the referendum has no validity, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean for the SDS activists to try to prevent --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bizarre if you are thinking in terms of democratic practices, but not necessarily if you are thinking in terms of this situation and their intentions and aspirations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The only people who accepted the proposition that the Serbs put forward that the referendum was invalid were other Serbs; the rest of the world saw the referendum as valid and acted upon it as if it were valid, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is broadly correct, although if you have read the Tadic case, then you will see that an academic colleague of mine, Robert Hayden, actually believes that that should not have been the case. Not everybody on the outside world.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That is true. Not everybody in the outside world. Nothing is agreed to by everybody in the outside world. But in any event as a result of that referendum, the Badinter Commission was satisfied that it was sufficient to constitute an expression of the will of the people of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the EC and its member states then proceeded to recognise the independent international personality of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On May 22nd 1992, the United Nations admitted Bosnia-Herzegovina putting the further stamp of international approval on the route it had taken as a state, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So that once Bosnia-Herzegovina had acquired this international recognition through the EC, the United States, and finally the United Nations, then any citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina who took up arms against that legitimate internationally recognised government could appropriately be termed rebels, could they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They could be termed rebels, but that is not the only way in which they might be termed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They could be termed a lot of things, but it may be more accurate to refer to them as Bosnian rebels than to refer to them as Serb forces, for instance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I doubt if it would be appropriate to refer to them as Bosnian rebels, although in one technical sense of that you could say that it is the case, but in a meaningful sense they regarded themselves as being Serbs rather than Bosnians in this context and therefore the rebellion, if that is the way you want to describe it, was not of Bosnians but of Serbs who were seeking, if anything, to reject some sense of that which was Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: For perhaps a few hundred years prior to that time, those Serbs who had been born in Bosnia, whose fathers had been born in Bosnia, whose grandfathers had been born in Bosnia, certainly recognised themselves as Bosnians and citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Another of these problematic expressions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They called themselves --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all I think the idea of citizenship of Bosnia-Herzegovina is not anything which can be said to be appropriate until the creation of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, within the Federal People's Republic of Yugoslavia or possibly even the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, that is from 1974, from which time at least they were issued with specific passports, so from which republic you came, you would have a BH passport or a Croatia passport or an Serbia passport, so in terms of citizenship, I would say it would be inappropriate to say they had these centuries of citizenship. It is clear that through periods of the 19th century and parts of the 20th century there were some who regarded themselves as Bosnians and in general in the former Yugoslavia people would refer to Bosnians, whether or not they were Serbs, Croats or Muslims but it is also the case, you can see this from events in 1976/88, that some of them regarded themselves as Orthodox, which also increasingly came to be associated as being Serb, as you pointed out yourself earlier, eastern Orthodox were the Serbs and this became the identity as Serbia became more and more a prominent state.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: To an extent they called themselves Bosnian Serbs, they voted in elections that were held in Bosnia-Herzegovina, they served in the Parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina, they held positions in the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina and they lived in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you are talking rather than for hundreds of years before, which I think is what you said about the latter period, then with the exception that I am not sure they necessarily called themselves Bosnian Serbs, that is the case. I might point out, not that I have expertise in anthropology, but anthropologists have noted that in Bosnia-Herzegovina the distinctions were made between Croat, Muslim and Orthodox, rather than between Croats, Muslims and Serbs, for most of the time. I say that with complete recognition, just for clarification in the use of the terminology and what they were deemed to call themselves, and without making any greater claim than the use of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If we go far enough back in history --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, in saying that, I am not going back in history, I am talking about research done in the 1980s.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But if we go far enough back in history, there are people who call themselves Muslim Croats living in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You can find people who call themselves many things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I do not know if you know this or not, and if you do not, you can just tell me and we can get there with someone else or in a different way, but do you know that citizenship of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, SFRY, was what is known as a derivative citizenship; in other words, to be a citizen of SFRY, you had to be recognised as a citizen of one of its republics; did you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say that I really know about citizenship and this idea of, what you say, derivative, but I think maybe I can get there by going back to my previous or last but one answer, in which I pointed out that there was a degree of attachment to each republic and if you had a SFRY passport, it stated your republic -- which republic you came from, designated your citizenship status, so each serial number would begin -- for example, for Bosnia-Herzegovina would be "BH".

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So to get a Yugoslav passport, you had to prove and demonstrate that you were a citizen of one of the republics, and that designation appeared on the passport?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the whole, but that designation which appeared was not necessarily that of the republic from which you came, always. I know of cases where people from Belgrade had BH passports, never having had anything to do with Bosnia-Herzegovina, I should point out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There are people going around with passports from places they have never been today. Those kind of things happen, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, I am just making that clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you want to be a citizen of Dominica, all you have to do is send them $50,000 and they will send you a passport. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know that, but thanks for the advice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You do not even have to go to Dominica. When we start talking about the breakout of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina and forces being assembled that wound up fighting each other, I think you will agree with me that the Bosnian government forces, those trying to defend the integrity of that newly independent state, were made up of virtually all the constituent ethnic population of Bosnia-Herzegovina; there were Muslims and Serbs and Croats and Jews and gypsies and virtually all the people that were living in Bosnia-Herzegovina to some extent were some of the Bosnian government army, TO or other organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whichever designation you use, then there were representatives from different communities in the armed forces. I think that is probably the first time I have heard of gypsies being involved, but I do not know that there were not gypsies either.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You are certainly familiar with General Divjak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know who General Divjak is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know he was a Bosnian Serb who formerly had been an officer in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do know that, and he was deputy commander of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So to refer to the Bosnian government forces as Muslim forces is a bit misleading also, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be technically inaccurate, the appropriate designation probably would be mainly Muslim, which is generally the way in which, if they are not described as the Bosnian government armed forces, the way to which they are referred.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Probably the best way to describe those forces are Bosnian government forces, because that was what they were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the best way to describe them, but it is not the only way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You talked yesterday about the Patriot League.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Patriotic League, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That group also contained Serbs and Croats.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It did, but again it was primarily Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When the rebellion broke out, not all of the Serbs living in Bosnia supported the rebel forces or participated on the side of the rebel forces, did they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they did not. I believe we have already established that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We have established that they did not support the Karadzic line, but when war actually started, they also did not participate in that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some did not, but I think we also established that some of them participated as members of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Tens of thousands of Serbs fled the country rather than become involved in fighting on behalf of the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Primarily, that was the better educated Serbs who were living in places like Banja Luka and places like that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That may well be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am at a perfect breaking point. I have a whole new subject to start at this point and this may be a good point to end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose your programme itself compelled you to stop, the programme you have been following, and you have reached the stage where you could not go forward. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think when we start -- Mr. Niemann, you suggested Dr. Gow is not staying beyond today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour, that was one of the difficulties I had foreshadowed, one of the reasons that I suggested I would not call Dr. Gow, because he cannot now be available until the next date in January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is all right. I think we will still have to tolerate that process. So many of these things have been going in pieces here, we have so many disjointed arrangements. We do not have it flowing the way we would want it. I think it depends on the next date which you will call him generally. I know you still have another expert witness tomorrow, do you not?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. That witness has arrived and will be ready to be called first thing in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: So goodbye Dr. Gow, we have not finished with you. I do not know whether we have even gone halfway, I am not sure. Whatever it is, we will continue with interesting questions and answers when you come back next time. It is an expert opinion we are expecting each time, so whenever you come, we hope to expect the best out of the whole exercise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are we at chapter two by now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for the time being. I think we will see you again. So the Trial Chamber will now rise and reassemble tomorrow morning. (5.30 pm)

procedural_notes.text: (Hearing adjourned until 10.00 am the following day)
